maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 RULING BY MR. SPEAKER ON PROCEDURAL ACCEPTABILITY OF CERTAIN BILLS

speechtext: On the order: Introduction of Bills.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 RULING BY MR. SPEAKER ON PROCEDURAL ACCEPTABILITY OF CERTAIN BILLS
speechtext:
Last week, a number of bills were proposed for introduction to the House. The Chair expressed reservations about certain procedural aspects of those bills. While three were then accepted for introduction after serious consideration, seven were held in abeyance. On Friday last, hon. members were given an opportunity to express views on a point of order which queried whether these bills might not affect the financial initiative of the Crown. A number of members participated in the interesting procedural debate and I have now had time to study their arguments.
The hon. member for Skeena suggested that the bills in question proposed to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and argued that they do not infringe upon the financial initiative of the Crown. The hon. member suggested that if in fact all these bills or any of them are found by the Chair to affect the Crown's prerogative in this respect, the rule should be disregarded as being archaic. The hon. member will appreciate, I am sure, that the Chair can hardly be expected to disregard a rule that is so fundamental. If in respect of any of these bills the Chair is convinced that the financial initiative of the Crown is in fact affected, it has no alternative but to set them aside. That is the conclusion which I have reached in connection with three of the seven bills in question.
The bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Broadview purports to be an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. In fact it is a bill to amend the Income Tax Act. Clause 1 repeals section 158(2) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, but clause 158(2) repeals section 10(l)(h) of the Income Tax Act so that in fact clause 1 of this bill should not set out that it repeals
section 158(2) of the Unemployment Insurance Act but that it repeals section 10(l)(h) of the Income Tax Act. The Unemployment Insurance Act says that benefits are taxable but the purpose of the bill is to make benefits nontaxable and to make workmen's compensation also nontaxable. This to my mind is purely taxation legislation and is not acceptable unless initiated by the Crown.
The bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West also purports to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act while in fact in my view it is an amendment to the Income Tax Act. The purpose of the bill according to the explanatory note is to make unemployment insurance non-taxable when the benefits are received by Indians living on a reserve. This of course affects the taxing initiative of the Crown and is out of order.
I have the same reservations concerning a bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Kootenay West. That bill proposes to change the method of payment of that part of claimants' benefits which is to be deducted at the source as taxable income. This again to my way of thinking deals clearly with tax legislation and as such is irregular unless introduced upon the initiative of the Crown.
I have extremely serious reservations about the four remaining bills. Generally speaking, these bills tend to increase the benefits payable under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act or to extend the period during which benefits might be payable under the law.
The question is whether legislation providing for such additional payments affects the financial initiative of the Crown and requires as a condition precedent the recommendation of the Crown. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has argued that amendments have been allowed where the purpose was to relieve individuals of taxation rather than to impose a tax on someone else. I do not disagree with those rulings which were made in committee; I point out, however, that they were amendments and not new initiatives as in the present case. Citation 265 of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition is the authority to establish that distinction.
I am more impressed by the argument advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and other hon. members that the moneys required for the payment of proposed extended benefits would not come out of the consolidated revenue fund and that they would not in any way affect the balance of ways and means. It is certainly a moot question whether these legislative proposals would in fact, in one way or another, directly or indirectly impose an additional burden on the public treasury and thus infringe upon the financial initiative of the Crown. One might well wonder whether government legislation tending to alter the benefits payable under the act or perhaps tending to shift the burden from one group of contributors to the other should not be accompanied by

March 27, 1972
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
the usual recommendation. I somewhat suspect that some hon. members in this House would insist that this kind of legislation, if it were sponsored by the government, should be accompanied by a recommendation.
At the same time, there are precedents, particularly in British parliamentary practice, which tend to indicate that such legislative proposals, because they do not, strictly speaking, impose a tax or an impost as referred to in Standing Order 62, are outside the rule which protects the financial initiative of the Crown.
Because of the difficulty in interpreting the statute which these bills propose to amend, and because these bills, if they had been included in the original group filed at the opening of the session, would now be before the House along with all the others, I feel it would be fair to give the sponsors of these four bills the benefit of the doubt. The conclusion would be that the two bills sponsored by the hon. member for Timiskaming, that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and that of the hon. member for Skeena would be acceptable for submission to the House at this time.
However, I have an additional reservation regarding the bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Skeena. This does not have to do with his use of Latin in his explanatory note but rather with another aspect of the explanatory note. It has been ruled that such notes ought to be an explanation and not an argument. The mover of a bill cannot introduce in his explanatory note the speech or the arguments he might want to present on second reading. Somehow, I feel that that is what the hon. member for Skeena has attempted in his explanatory note which to some extent is poetry. It sounds lyrical to the Chair. I strongly urge the hon. member to make his explanatory note conform more with existing practice and the form that is usual for such explanatory notes. That is the only reservation I would have in connection with his bill. I hope the hon. member will find it possible to make the necessary correction, perhaps in consultation with learned parliamentary counsel, after which the bill could be introduced. The other three bills standing in the name of the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre can be introduced at this time.

wan Wheat Pool that to meet export grain commitments from west coast ports 800 cars will have to be unloaded daily, and at Thunder Bay 1,700 daily after May 1, and that this level will have to be maintained through to November, can the minister responsible for the Wheat Board inform the House whether he has received any commitment from the CNR and the CPR to provide the equipment which would enable these levels to be maintained?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
maintopic: PROVISION OF EQUIPMENT BY RAILWAYS TO MEET EXPORT COMMITMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the figures quoted might perhaps even be considered minimum requirements in view of the tremendous sales prospects for Canadian grain. The Wheat Board has held discussions with the railroads and so have members of the government. We shall be continuing to hold such discussions. The railways have indicated the number of cars they are able to provide in connection with the movement of grain. The number of unloadings that can be accomplished tends to depend in part on the manner in which the system as a whole operates, the manner in which the terminals and the elevators operate. As I say, discussions are continuing. I expect to have a further meeting in a week or so with the railways and the elevator companies in connection with this matter.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned last Friday I was saying that the first duty of a responsible government is to provide the funds necessary to ensure satisfactory operation of the economic life of Canadians. I know that some people may accuse me of again talking about money. In fact, did the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) himself not talk of this all through his speech-and yet, none of my colleagues will blame him for it.
I said before that we live in society in order to be assured of a greater opportunity for comfort and wellbeing, and I must add that the government which society has chosen is in a sense a board of directors which manages common funds and which should govern from above as a sovereign and supreme adjudicator, with complete impartiality, and only in the interest of the common good and of justice.
In 1971, the members of our society produced through their work about $95 billion worth of products, but because of the modernization of our means of production and of our association, the buying power distributed between the members of society during this production cycle is lower than the volume of production, which shows that there are surpluses.
The board of directors-i.e., the government-should therefore distribute this surplus equitably by issuing new funds-that is, by increasing the volume of buying power in the same proportion and at the same rate as Canadians

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
increase production-in order to ensure a satisfactory economic life for Canada.
Society is a type of federalism within which an economic system is established. Ours is a capitalist system which is not bad in itself, but has been distorted. Its structure, though, is sound. However, order is violated when capital always receives the largest reward and the people are but a means of enhancing still more the money capital with no regard for the rights of human capital, of human dignity or of the social nature of economic activity, or even of social justice and common good.
To be true to ourselves and just towards others, Parliament has the duty to recognize that in order to effectively participate in this capitalist system, everyone should necessarily enjoy a basic capital, that is a capital related to his individual and family responsibilities, otherwise we contribute to a greater distortion of the capitalist system.
This system is in need of reform and it will be reformed by men of order with and for us, or else without and against us.
If accepted, the economic and social security systems proposed by the Social Credit party of Canada would already amount to a most worthy reform since Canadian families would receive a supplementary capital enabling them to share in Canada's plenty.
We have already shown that due to the increase of the cost of living, it has become necessary to increase to $5,000 the tax exemption for a married couple plus $500 for each child, and to $2,500 for a single taxpayer.
We have also shown that it would be possible to give family allowances of $250 a year for children 17 years of age or less and to make available an initial capital of $1,200 to those 18 and over.
Since participation in our capitalist system requires capital and most younger people do not have any besides whatever money they can save on their salary and since it is presently impossible for a great many to find a job, there is no more efficient means than the one we propose. And they can double, triple and produce even more with that capital which is practically a minimum, and the whole country will benefit from it.
This formula would accomplish the opposite of what welfare and unemployment insurance do, both of which force recipients to remain inactive and unproductive.
Achieving this plan will require money and in order not to strip those who are working and paying taxes, there is only one way: our sovereign government should regain the right to cash in on our credit by setting up a national credit board which would guide the Bank of Canada. This way we would have a truly social credit instead of a debt credit as is the case now.
High finance servants sometimes retort that if that were possible, it would have been done in other countries. Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out a fact that happened in the United States a little more than a 100 years ago, under president Abraham Lincoln.
International finance at that time had taken possession of America as well as Europe, keeping constant watch

over its positions. One man dared one day insult it. He had to pay with his life. It was, I believe, the greatest president of the United States.
He was the son of a settler and never had the chance to go to school. But having learned to read from his mother and having studied law at night, after his hard day in the woods or in the fields, Lincoln finally became president of the United States at a critical time when the North and the South were at war.
Gifted with a staunch common sense and led by an unequalled rectitude of mind, Lincoln considered that if private banks make money and have people accept it, while passing it as debts, a sovereign government could make it as well and give it at least the same flexibility. So he asked the Treasury Secretary Chase to float successively three issues totalling $450 million in 1862-1863.
In 1938, after a legal fight between financial powers and the government, $346 were still in circulation, and had the same value as bank money.
Better still, contrary to the bankers' debt money, Lincoln's "greenbacks" did not saddle the United States public debt with one single dollar.
Had this issue come through the ordinary channel of banks, it would have increased the United States public debt from 1863 to 1938 by $10 billion, including compound interest. Were all their money issued by the government in that way, the United States would have no public debt.
The same can be said about Canada. The very existence of a public debt is the evidence of a defective system, of the money being corrupt right from the beginning.
This is why we are clamouring for a monetary reform while it is still time. I am sure that our reform proposals in this field would lead to a restoration of our social economic system and put an end to the jurisdiction conflict in fiscal matters between the federal government and the provinces. And more time could be devoted to other sectors of administration, in the best interests of all Canadians.

Mr. ]ames A. McGrath (St. John's East): Mr. Speaker, there are serious discrepancies between the bill presently before us and the bill on the same topic introduced in the last session. That, I think, was Bill C-264, and it died when the session ended. In that bill, the government committed itself to increasing the benefits on May 1, 1972. Every week from the moment that bill was introduced in September of last year, until the end of the session, members of the House asked the government to bring that legislation forward. I am thinking particularly of mv colleaeue from Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) in this regard. On behalf of our party, he put forward a number of suggestions to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) that this bill be brought forward so that parliament could deal with it, since there was a general disposition in the House to pass it. Certainly, every member of this House was in favour of that legislation. Why the government did not proceed with the bill remains one of the great mysteries of this parliament.
March 27, 1972

The government has introduced a similar legislative proposal designated as Bill C-170 in the present session. There are a number of departures from provisions contained in the old bill, of which the most serious is the one to which I am about to allude. Under the bill now before the House, the government has discretionary power as to when the provisions of the bill regarding the payment of the new benefits will be implemented. Frankly, I am not happy about this, because I do not trust the government. I have already said that I do not see why provisions such as those this bill contains could not now be in force. The government has no legitimate excuse for not bringing them forward. There is no reason why families in Canada, especially the lower income families, should not now be enjoying the benefits of this bill. Consequently, I fail to understand why the government has refused to commit itself to a target date for implementation, as it did in the bill introduced in the previous session.
The government wants to leave the door open, so that proclamation of this legislation, once it has been passed by parliament, can be kept in abeyance until the election is called. Then, payments could be made to families in Canada a few days before the next federal election. I consider that to be the real motive behind that particular change in the bill, and it is regrettable. I feel that the needed benefits under this legislation should now be going to families in Canada, many of which desperately need these increased benefits.
In September, 1958, the Economic Council of Canada reported:
Poverty in Canada is real. Its numbers are not in the thousands, but the millions. There is more of it than our society can tolerate, more than our economy can afford, and far more than existing measures and efforts can cope with.
I have just read an excerpt from the Economic Council's report on poverty, published in 1968. Obviously, the poverty problem was too large and, indeed, too painful to ignore. On May 21, 1968, in Stratford, Ontario, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised during the election campaign that new financial plans he would make would be directed at the poor. It is interesting to note that, as a first step in fulfilling this promise, the government directed the Deputy Minister of National Health and Welfare to undertake a review of existing social policies. His report was accompanied by a series of recommendations, but unfortunately that report was never made public.
By November 30, 1970, two and a half years after the election, the government introduced a white paper on income security. It contained three main proposals, the first of which recommended a doubling of family allowances for all families with incomes of less than $4,500. Those with incomes between $4,500 and $10,000 would receive allowances on a sliding scale. Families with incomes over $10,000 would receive nothing.
On the basis of Bill C-264 introduced in the previous session, that being a bill similar to Bill C-170,1 sent out a circular to constituents of mine living in the rural parts of my district. I asked them to tell me by return mail the number of children they had and the size of their existing family allowance cheques. I said I would calculate for them, on the basis of the bill then before us, how much they could each expect to receive in new benefits if and
Family Income Security Plan when parliament passed that legislation. About 90 per cent of the people who responded to my survey qualified for maximum benefits, because their income level kept them below the requirements set out in the bill. Of the 10 per cent who could not expect to receive maximum benefits, payments, in the majority of cases, would be cut by only $3 or $5; that is, if you were over the income ceiling, benefits would be reduced by 33 cents for each $100 of income over that ceiling. Thus, since the incomes of those people perhaps were $1,000 or $2,000 over the income ceiling, benefits would be reduced by, say, between $3 and $5 per month.
However, Mr. Speaker, the point is that only a handful of people were to be cut off completely because their incomes were so high. A very small percentage, as I say, were to be cut off completely because their income level was so high that they could not expect to receive benefits. This group formed a very, very small percentage of the whole. I admit that Newfoundland is probably unique in this respect. We have large families. Statistically, I think, the largest families in the country are to be found in Newfoundland. Probably, the percentage of our population under 16 years of age is the largest in the country. I think one can include Quebec in these figures, although I am not sure. So, most families with large numbers of children could expect to benefit from this legislation and receive substantially increased payments. Also, Mr. Speaker, the increased payments would represent a substantial supplemental source of income for many of these people. Many of these families, largely because of their size and often because the breadwinner has been unemployed, unfortunately have had to depend on welfare payments made under the Canada Assistance Plan. As I say, these increased benefits would represent to them an important supplemental source of income. For them, Mr. Speaker, this legislation is an absolute necessity.
Although there have been some improvements in legislative proposals, the government seems to have dragged its feet on major recommendations. In replying to the white paper, the National Council on Welfare said that the government still has not shown a social philosophy which is directed towards ending poverty in Canada. I submit that comment for the consideration of the minister, in order that the government can develop that philosophy, can develop an over-all plan to do something about the serious matter of poverty in this country.
Although the Economic Council of Canada issued its report on poverty almost four years ago, the family income security plan which was drafted late in 1970 and was to revise the Family Allowances Act, is still being changed at this late date. I do not doubt that by the time we get to the committee stage with this bill, there will be further changes in the form of government amendments. That seems to be the pattern this government has followed with legislation introduced in this House. No attempt has been made to sort out the problems that will develop under the family income security plan as a result of certain provisions of the Canada Assistance plan. I am not at all satisfied with the minister's references to this aspect. They were far too limited, bearing in mind the scope of the problems that could develop.

Under the Canada Assistance Plan, and the minister knows this, the provinces are entitled to lower their rates of welfare assistance to families. They can lower these rates in proportion to the higher family allowance payments that will be made under this program. There is a great danger of that happening. The minister has not been able to satisfy the House that the provinces will not indeed be tempted to do just that.
It is rather interesting to note that the Canada Assistance Plan, which is one of the main social programs of the government, has been the subject of study for some considerable time. The provinces have made a number of representations to the government at federal-provincial conferences. Indeed, a number of representations have been made to the government in this House, asking for changes in the Canada Assistance Plan. For some strange reason, the government seems loathe to do so. One can only conclude that the government lacks an over-all social philosophy, an over-all sense of direction as to exactly where we are going with regard to the problem of poverty which we have in this land of plenty.
According to the Economic Council of Canada, there are five million Canadians whom they have designated as living below the poverty line. In this regard, it is rather interesting to note that large families constitute the majority of the poor in this country. Of those who are designated as poor, 23.3 per cent have families with four or more children under 16 years of age. That group represents by far the largest portion of those who qualify as being poor under the definition of the Economic Council of Canada in the province of Newfoundland.
Another aspect that concerns me, and this was alluded to by my colleague, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), is the eroding effect of inflation on the social welfare payments. People on fixed incomes, people who depend to a disproportionate extent on family allowances and that kind of social assistance as a very important part of their income, suffer most from the erosion of the dollar by inflation. These are the people who really have to suffer from the consequences of inflation. It is interesting to note that since the initial dollar amounts for family allowances were set in 1945, when the average weekly wage in Canada was about $32.50, the average weekly industrial wage has increased more than four times that level. In 1970, the average weekly wage in Canada was $132.72. However, in contrast to this more than 300 per cent increase, the average family allowance per child has only gone up by 15 per cent since 1945.
Therefore, simply to restore the original relative relationship of family allowances to wages, the proposed maximum FISP payments should be even larger than the $180 a year now proposed for ages 0-11 and the $240 a year proposed for ages 12-17. Rather, it appears that the maximum annual FISP amounts needed to restore the shrinkage over the years in the relative size of these baby bonus payments would be at least $257 and $334. In each case, the proposed FISP maximum payment amounts are less than 75 per cent of these updated amounts. As a result, far from representing an advance and breaking new ground, the Family Income Security Plan will merely restore part of what has been lost because of inflation and

even then, because of the selectivity in the scheme that will cut off families in higher income brackets, only some will be able to regain the lost ground.
There is another way of viewing the erosion of the family allowance dollar since the 1945 inception of the plan, and that is to look at the effect of inflation on the family allowance dollar from that date. Between July, 1945 and September, 1971, when Bill C-264 was introduced into the House of Commons, the Consumer Price Index had more than doubled, reaching 230.7. If the amount of the baby bonus cheques had kept pace with this rise, the payment for a child, for example age 11, would have risen from $7 a month in July 1945 to $16.15 a month in September, 1971. Instead, a child aged 11 will be receiving, if and when Bill C-170 in its present form and with the same payment schedule is finally passed, a maximum of $15 a month, and most children aged 11 will be receiving much less or nothing at all.
I would like to get back to the relationship of this bill to the Canada Assistance Plan. I do not think enough has been said about that. The Canada Assistance Plan contains provisions that, unless remedial action is taken before FISP is enacted, could undermine completely the objective of the bill before the House. The only way we can be reassured in this regard is for the minister to undertake to negotiate with the provinces to obtain an agreement with them that there will be no reduction in welfare assistance. The problem in a nutshell, as I already said, is that under the Canada Assistance Plan, the provinces are entitled to lower their rates of welfare assistance to families in proportion to the higher family allowance payments these families will be receiving under this proposed legislation. There is nothing in the present plan to stop them from doing that.
Under the present Canada Assistance Plan, many provinces find it an increasing burden to meet their commitments. In my own province of Newfoundland, the 50 per cent portion of welfare payments which the province must pay represents a very disproportionate part of our budget. My province finds it very difficult to continue to assume this burden. We must bear in mind that we have the highest rate of unemployment in the country. This is a direct consequence of the federal government's failure to implement proper policies to combat inflation and to implement proper policies to combat regional disparity. It is because of the shortcomings of federal policies in this regard that Newfoundland has a higher rate of unemployment than any other province in Canada and, consequently, we have a much larger proportion of our population on welfare than any other province.
Under Section 2(b)(iii) of the Canada Assistance Plan, there is a provision that the provinces, in determining the degree of need and arrangements for social assistance to applicants for welfare, shall take into account all income maintenance payments through unemployment insurance, old age pension security, Canada Pension Plan and Guaranteed Income Supplement schemes. However, it is optional for the provinces to take into account family allowance and other schemes; this is a decision for each individual province to make. Because of the exceptionally high welfare payments that many provinces are forced to make because of unprecedented high unemployment, we
March 27, 1972

wonder how many provinces will be tempted to take advantage of that provision which exists in the Canada Assistance Plan. Apparently none of the provinces now include family allowance payments in calculating income for purposes of assistance. However, it is possible and, indeed, highly probable, that after the family income security plan becomes law, and higher benefits are paid to larger families, several of the provinces will do just that: they will include family income security payments as part of a welfare applicant's income and will reduce social assistance payments correspondingly. This is especially likely to happen in the case of the poorer provinces.
Not only does the new family income security plan fail, in my opinion, to close the gap between the buying power of the allowance in 1945 as compared with the present buying power of the family allowance cheque, but in future the gap may become even greater in the absence from the plan of an automatic escalation clause in accordance with which payments would increase as inflation takes effect in the future. Although the present bill, unlike its predecessor, contains a clause providing for an increase in benefit levels and payments as the cost of living increases, the procedure is not automatic. I believe it should be. After all, we do not know who will be minister when the present minister leaves office.
A matter of this kind should not be left to the discretion of any minister. After all, regardless of the extent to which these men may be socially committed or how conscious they may be of the need, they will still have to persuade their colleagues in the cabinet of the necessity for granting increases. I feel, therefore, that the bill should contain a clause making the escalations mandatory. The lack of an automatic escalator clause in the present legislation means that neither benefit levels nor benefit payments take into account the eroding effect which inflation will exert in the future. Only a few days ago the Chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission stated that inflation was still a very serious problem. And inflation will continue to be a serious problem. Consequently, we feel it is unforgivable on the part of the government to fail to take this fact of life into account when drafting legislation designed to end poverty and make it easier for families on low incomes to live.
Since 1961, personal income per capita has almost doubled, rising from $1,613 to $3,092 a year. This does not mean that fewer people are living in poverty. Inflation has considerably eroded the buying power of the dollar in the last ten years. Though personal incomes have risen, cutoff lines for both maximum and partial family income benefit payments are stationary. If personal incomes double again in the course of the next ten years, increasing numbers of people will find themselves disqualified in respect of FISP payments, their incomes having risen above the stationary cut-off lines. Yet many of these people may still be defined by Statistics Canada or the Economic Council of Canada as living below the poverty line.
I do not object to the ending of the universality aspect of the plan. Until Canada reaches the stage at which we are prepared to co-ordinate all the social welfare activities of our various governments in the field of family allowances,
25104-15 J
Family Income Security Plan
old age pensions, blind persons pensions, veterans pensions and so on, and put some order into the chaos which presently exists by agreeing to some kind of guaranteed income arrangement, or negative income tax, if that is more acceptable, I have no quarrel with the government's proposal to end the universal application of family allowance payments. I say this because there are families in this country which do not need these family allowance payments, while there are other families who desperately need an improvement in their position, and I have in mind the majority of the poorer families.
It is interesting to note that two of the ten provinces already operate their own supplemental family allowance programs. I presume that negotiations have taken place in this connection between the federal government and the government of Quebec. I believe the minister referred to this. But I wonder whether discussions have taken place with the government of Newfoundland with respect to the supplemental program operated by that province. It is understandable, and in many instances necessary, that provinces should supplement federal social welfare programs, thereby exercising their constitutional option in this field. Since 1966, Newfoundland has provided a benefit amounting to $15 per year per child attending schools other than trade schools or universities. In 1967, the Quebec government also established a provincial program to supplement family allowances in respect of all children below the age of 16.
In conclusion, I trust that when he replies to questions during the clause by clause study of the bill at the committee stage the minister will reassure us on these points. I trust he will tell us, for example, that he has received commitments from the provinces that they will not exercise their option under the Canada Assistance Plan to reduce welfare payments proportionate to the increase which may be provided under this program. I hope he will be able to tell us, also, that the plan will not interfere with existing provincial programs such as those in effect in Newfoundland and Quebec, or with programs which may be contemplated by other provinces. Finally, I hope that the minister, who I believe to be personally committed to this principle, will be able to tell us in general terms when we may expect to see all the social welfare programs in Canada co-ordinated to the point at which we shall be able to take that final step which I believe to be so necessary, that is, to bring in some form of guaranteed income. In my opinion, this is the only way in which we can end poverty in this country.

It is a little like your feeling toward a leaky umbrella in a heavy rainstorm. You have to use it because it is the only protection available, but you sure wish you had an umbrella without holes, one which would really do the job.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
In our view this is a very shabby substitute for an adequate system of social security, and before I finish I hope to explore a few of the holes through which I believe the rain is bound to enter.
The hon. member who preceded me, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), said that he did not object to the doing away with the universality feature, because until such time as we could have a co-ordinated guaranteed income system we would probably have to put up with the selectivity system. I would point out to him that this bill is a retreat from the principle of universality that we have been moving toward over the years. It is a retreat from the concept of a Canadianism that could stretch from coast to coast and embrace every citizen, without regard to race, class, place or creed. Under this concept of universality, which up to a certain point in Canadian history we had been achieving, people pay taxes according to ability to pay. This is measured by their income. Universal benefits they receive without distinction. These benefits are then taxed back according to ability to pay of the recipient, as I say, measured by their income. It is simple, it is uncomplicated, it is fair and it works.
I remember that the old age pension legislation began in a restrictive way. Originally, the pension was $20 a month payable at age 70, and there was a means test. This test is now politely dignified by use of the term "selectivity". Over the years pensions were made universal, and this was finally achieved in 1951. Indeed, this universality was gradually broadened, as we know, to include people within a lower age bracket, until finally those who were 65 received the pension. Then began the restrictions which I will come to in a moment.
What this universal pension meant in terms of freedom, independence and human dignity was wonderful to behold. Prior to the universal old age pension, prior to even the partial pension, our elderly people during the years which preceded the great depression were forced to go to court to prove their children were not able to support them before they were given any public funds at all. Many of our elderly people were mortified at doing this. They were ashamed and hurt that they had to take their children to court and rob those children's families in order to get funds so they could receive support, if the court so ordered.
Finally, as a civilized country, we got to the stage of saying that this must not be; that the people who had built this country had a right to be independent, free, to have their dignity preserved and protected by a pension of their own. Then, later on we introduced family allowances. We went to the other end of the age scale and said that young children have a right to be independent and to be helped financially in the same way; that their parents have the right to bring them up properly and preserve their health, wellbeing and dignity. Thus, we instituted the family allowance program, children's allowances, on a universal basis.
Over the years there has been practically no case of cheating or dishonesty. I know this is a fact, because each year we question the officials before the health and wel-

fare committee and this is what they tell us. While this method of universal family allowances provided a measure of security for our children, it also provided for their mothers a recognition of the value of the service they gave. I shall come back to that a little later.
It now seems that this government is determined to turn universal legislation into class legislation. I know the government dignifies it with the term "selectivity", but selectivity requires a means test. It means that people will be degraded and demeaned, that they will be marked with a stigma just as horrible as the stigma that marks those who have to live in the high rise ghettos built for people on low incomes, ghettos in which it is so terrible for families to live. The government uses honeyed words to disguise the sharp sting of means test legislation.

My authority for this statement lies with people who at that time were bringing up families. I have never understood why, from the standpoint of sanity, efficiency and sound administration, it was ever found necessary to depart from that simple and just way of doing things. March 27, 1972

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, please do not let the minister tempt me. If he does I shall have to give him another wedge of quotations from the Canadian Council on Social Development, and I do not want to have to do that because I am sure he knows those quotations as well as I. If he did not he would not have paraphrased them the other day and thus avoided some rather awkward quotations. The minister knows the Canadian Council on Social Development wants universality of payment without discrimination, without a means test, and it wants selectivity of taxation according to a person's ability to pay.
I see the minister shaking his head so I cannot avoid quoting the council. They state:
Family allowances should be universal, paid to all families with dependent children as a social right thus avoiding divisiveness among families and any element of stigma. The present program has this feature but FISP would eliminate it.
Let me tell the minister that I am not paraphrasing but quoting directly. The government will not accept this principle. If you would like to know why, Mr. Speaker, all you need do is take a look at the tax bill, Bill C-169, which we dealt with recently. It provided a few dollars for the poor, many for the wealthy and a bonanza for certain forms of corporate wealth-oil, gas, and similar companies. In other words, in the tax system there is anything but equality and fairness. We had the Carter Report which recommended that people be taxed strictly on the amount of income they have. This very elaborate and comprehensive report was shoved into a filing cabinet early in the game. This is obvious because Bill C-169 does not tax on the basis of ability to pay. Even before the introduction of Bill C-169, this government was taxing not on the ability to pay but heavily in respect of those people who could least afford to pay and who were the most defenseless. The government has now found it necessary to take the steps it has taken toward scrapping universality in social security schemes.
The government's first retreat from universality was in respect of old age pension legislation. It divided old age pensioners of this country into two categories, the poor and the destitute. The government said to the poor it would allow a 42 cent increase in pension bringing it up to $80 per month, and it would remain at this figure in perpetuity or for as long as the Liberal government was in power. I hope the two will not last for the same length of time. I doubt if they will.
The appeal to destroy federal universality made by the minister over and over again when he spoke the other day is made to the heavily burdened lower and middle income groups, particularly to the one-third middle income taxpayers who are taxed more heavily now than they should be. The middle income third is taxed more heavily because this government will not tax the upper third the way it should be taxed. Consequently, this middle income group is groaning under its heavy tax burden, but the minister says to them that one place the government can really save is in that area of federal universality in respect of family allowances. He suggests the poor people need these allowances and that is where the money should go. In this way the middle income group will not have to pay as much tax. I think this is the area from which comes the
Family Income Security Plan
motivation of the government to destroy the universal feature of family allowances.
The minister introduced this bill as a strictly anti-poverty plan. I suggest that this government first impoverishes the people and then stigmatizes them. They will be impoverished because of the tax legislation and then they will be stigmatized. The minister says that the present family allowance figures of $72 to $120 are inadequate. No one quarrels with him in that regard. We all applauded his remarks that these amounts were insufficient to cover the annual cost of maintaining a child. The present figures are insufficient for this purpose as will be the prospective figures, and I will come to that later. The minister really overbid himself when he said that the primary goal of the present program is human development. I do not think this plan will do anything at all in the way of human development. It might help human survival, but that is all it will do. Forcing people with families to squeeze through the eye of the poverty needle is not the way to accomplish human development.
Let me deal with the faults of this legislation as I see them. First, this legislation divides people into categories of poor and indigent. This fault is similar to one in respect of old age pension legislation. It is mean, selective and discriminatory legislation, and we have heard how this works out in respect of those people near the borderline.
Second, it is extremely complex legislation and will be unworkable in many respects. It contains too many sliding scales and other special features which must be taken into account. The number of children, the size of benefits and the amount of income must be taken into account as well as what is and what is not income, and: there is a sliding scale in respect of payment. All these will make the legislation unworkable, as compared to the simple method of handing out universal benefits and taking them back through a nice, clean, computer technique. One can easily imagine the morass of bureaucracy this new measure will create.
Many people will be faced with these terrible and endless mathematical computations involving the number of children and other factors to which I have referred. Perhaps many of them will decide to have fewer children rather than be faced with these calculations. This family allowance legislation is so far removed from a method of adequately increasing benefits to big families that it may have the salutary effect of reducing the number of them. People may decide the calculations with which they are faced are too great in comparison with the benefits they may receive.
Third, just as in old age security pension legislation, there is no escalator clause in this bill. This is serious because the cost of living is going up relentlessly. Every forecast we see from the United States and from this country indicates that the cost of living will continue to move up in this fashion. How does this government justify the lack of an escalator clause in respect of security allowances with the lack of such a provision in this legislation?
Fourth, we must also consider the administrative cost of this program. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) estimated that this measure would require administratively 1,500 new public servants and would cost

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
in the neighbourhood of $12 million per year. I heard no denial from the minister who was here in the House when that statement was made. Nor did I hear a denial when the member said he calculated that under this type of program a recipient would receive about 9 cents of every dollar put aside for benefits. Great administrative armies are wonderful from the point of view of those armies, but they are pretty awful for the civilian population dependent upon these activities. This increased administrative cost will open the way for more red tape such as we have experienced in respect of other recent programs.
Fifth, let me refer to the impact of this legislation on those one million mothers who will not receive family allowances. Some 30.1 per cent of our mothers will be above the allowable level for the purpose of family allowance benefits. One might suggest they do not need these allowances. Let me point out that for many years all mothers in this country have been accustomed to these allowances. Many of them are in the low income groups and have had to use these allowances for urgent things such as food, clothing and rent. A great many mothers in the low and middle income groups have, by sacrifice, set aside the whole or a part of the family allowance cheque to pay for the educating of their children. Many women higher up on the income scale have set aside every family allowance cheque for the purpose of educating their children. For far too many women of either the high or low income group, the family allowance cheque has been the only source of ready cash which they could call their own.
This government has, through a very shortsighted, penny-pinching piece of legislation, swept these benefits from not only families in this country but from millions of mothers who have been setting aside these allowance cheques for various worthy purposes. This government has managed to alienate a good many sections of the population by its policy over the last few years, namely, the wheat farmers in the west, the fishermen down in the Maritimes, and quite a number of other people. I did not know that the government was quite prepared to adopt such a measure cutting off a million mothers across this country, but evidently that is what they are doing.
In case you might say that I am iust making a plea for the one million mothers who are in the higher income brackets, let me say that I will also urge you to look at the low-income mother who has to work outside her home, either because she is the single support of her family or because her husband does not earn enough money by himself to be able to provide for that family. Let us consider a mother getting $4,500 or a little more which qualifies her for family allowance. In order to go out to work she must hire babysitters. At $15 a week, which is certainly what she will have to pay to get most babysitters, she will be paying $780 a year. The most she can possibly get in family allowance for a child under 12 is $180 a year. What is this measure doing for the working woman who must work outside the home and hire babysitting services?
I am pointing this out to indicate that this measure is no great bonanza. By penalizing one million mothers in the upper income bracket in order to be able to get enough money for the other children, the primary goal of human

development will not be achieved. That may be the goal, but the minister will shoot so wide off the mark that he will forget where the target was. The minister may say that under Bill C-169 there is some provision for women who may get only partial family allowances for their children, but I want to point out that under the child care allowance provisions many women will be excluded from obtaining the deduction. I know that a woman in the $4,500 bracket who pays less than $500 in income tax does not qualify for a child care allowance deduction. When I was in Halifax about ten days ago a man with a family on a very low subsistence wage told me that he does not qualify for the $500 child care allowance deduction because he does not have enough income. So no one can tell me that the child care provisions in the Income Tax Act will partially make up to those families who do not receive the whole family allowance.
Let us consider a woman who is doing babysitting. Suppose she is married and suppose she earns $800 a year by babysitting. She must now declare her earnings and her husband must deduct her earnings from his exemption of $1,350 a year. On an average income that means that the babysitter's family unit will lose at least $137.50 cash on the husband's income tax return. So, the sitter assumes constant care and responsibility for a child for approximately 2400 working hours a year and earns, after her husband's taxes are deducted, only $600 instead of $800. Therefore, she receives exactly 24 cents an hour for her work. So, please do not tell me that the child care provisions will make up to those families who are unable to qualify for the family allowance.
I think this is a pretty poor deal all around. It is a hodgepodge, it is a bureaucratic jungle, it is a tangle of red tape, compared with what could be done if only this government would look at the economics of taxing people according to the amount of income they have, giving them universal, non-discriminatory family allowances and then taxing their income to the extent of taking back the whole family allowance and more if they do not need it.
The minister asks what the difference is. There may not be any difference to the minister, but let me tell him that there is a world of difference to the people who are on the receiving end because they would know that they are getting a non-discriminatory, fair amount and that they are paying for it. What they should pay is what their income indicates they must pay, and nothing more. We would not be going in for these unnecessary civil servants, the unnecessary paper work, the unnecessary computation and calculation and all the other things which only result in disguising the truth of the matter which is that this government is using measures of taxation which shield the wealthy. Then, they try to sell the poorer people on a scheme which does not protect them in anything like the measure to which they are entitled and which the wealth of this country, properly taxed, could give them.
In the Speech from the Throne which opened this session of parliament on February 17, the government included the following sentence:
In a period dominated by bigness, in an increasingly impersonal social system, one of the major challenges facing government is to remove the impression of isolation which so often surrounds men and women, depriving them of their sense of worth, of accom-
March 27, 1972

plishment, of fulfilment, and removing from them their identity as individuals.
In thinking of those one million Canadian mothers who will be excluded and those millions of mothers on very low income who are forced to go out to work and to hire babysitters, which costs so much more than the family allowance will give them, one is compelled to wonder why this government was finally driven to take this step of alienating all these women and at the same time destroying the universal character of family allowances. I hope that when this measure goes into committee and when we have a chance to look at it closely clause by clause, the minister may yet see what he is doing to the fabric of Canadian life; how this measure will downgrade and give lower priority to the job of homemaking and motherhood which we have been trying to raise in the eyes of the Canadian people. For years a small badge of status has been accorded to women in this country for bringing up their families, and a certain amount of help has been given them through family allowances. This has meant a great deal to women in all groups and in all income classes across this country. Let me beg the minister not to destroy the unity and good will of those mothers, but to use the opportunity and the second chance that he will get in the committee to make yet another modification in the family allowance legislation to bring it into line with the kind of family allowance legislation that is wanted by the Canadian Labour Congress, the National Council of Welfare, the Canadian Council on Social Development, and all the fathers and mothers across the country. Let us make this our greatest effort and experience in human growth and development.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about Bill C-170. May I first say I have always believed that any effort made to raise the income of the lower income group should be supported. I have also always believed that, so far as income is concerned, the goal of the individual is to reach higher. I have also believed that when increasing the income of the lower income group we should not do so by forcing a reduction in the income of those in the higher income group. I do not believe in a system where the have-nots take away from the haves until all are have-nots.
There are two areas of concern in Bill C-170. The first is the lack of an automatic cost of living escalator clause. The discretionary cost of living clause provided in the bill is inadequate, and inferior to an automatic escalator clause because it does not take into account the automatic erosion effect that inflation will have in the future. Inflation has always meant steady erosion in the buying power of the family allowance dollar and the pension dollar.
My second concern is the sliding scale by which the cut-off point is established at over $10,000. This calculation includes the husband's and wife's gross income, no matter what their expenses total. Working wives welcomed the latest tax reform legislation which provided compensation through deductions for day-care costs for their children. The new Unemployment Insurance Act provides for maternity benefits to be paid to women while they are away from work having their children. These two
Family Income Security Plan
reforms provided an incentive to women to remain on the job.
FISP takes a negative approach by penalizing working wives since the cut-off levels are based on gross family income. If a wife decides to work in order to supplement her husband's salary and help meet payments on their home, furniture, car, etc., it is more than likely that she will push the total family income above the cut-off level and forfeit part or all of her family allowance. Cut-off levels should be based on net income after deductions rather than on gross income, and the number of children in the family. I, personally, know people in the over $10,000 a year bracket who, because of their position, own a home and a car, and who must meet heavy mortgage payments and municipal taxes. After all their deductions and monthly payments, they are left in poverty so far as food and clothing are concerned.
What about a family with three to six or more children whose gross income is a little over $10,000? Surely these matters should be taken into consideration. The cut-off point should depend on how many people in a family have to work to earn the gross income. If a man is making $6,300, his wife makes over $3,800, and they have three children, they will lose an amount of $406 a year. This is actually a loss of income. It is a penalty. A couple with six children will lose $800 of income from both the federal and provincial governments. It is a penalty for those who try to reach a higher standard.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a bill whose principle is good. It is imperative to talk about increasing family allowances. Such an objective should have been dealt with quite sooner. Legislation providing for the payment of benefits in respect of children, Mr. Speaker, is evidently fine in principle.
I must however point out, as did other hon. members, its deficiencies: First, it is not sufficient enough since-and it must be admitted-benefits for children are increased to $15 and $20. This would add a bit to the extremely low amounts which families have been entitled to for many years, but it stills falls far short. There could be a comparison, for instance, with what a welfare service awards for the care of fosterchild.
Mr. Speaker, under the present welfare system in Quebec, approximately $40 to $50 per month are allocated for the care of a child under 6 years of age. At age 16 and 17, the amount awarded is $95 to $100 per month. Such provincial welfare legislation makes it possible for a woman-taking care of three or four children, for instance, who are not hers-to receive welfare benefits which really assist in the care of those dependent children.
But the defect in the system, and the proof of inadequacy of amounts granted under Bill C-170, is that families are faced with the following dilemma: a mother of three or four children whose income is inadequate, whether she is a widow or separated or her husband has disappeared for some reason or other, will receive from the welfare service only a pension of $150, $160, at the very most $200, which is already inadequate. She will receive family allowances of $15 or $20, as the case may be, under this

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
bill. On the other hand, if this mother were callous enough to abandon her children, whoever would be entrusted with their care would receive $50, $60 and up to $100 per month per child.
Mr. Speaker, one thing is sure and certain: if the mother were allowed to keep her own children, with a guarantee of adequate payments, there would no longer be the problem of this considerable number of children who now have to be placed in so-called foster homes.
It is ridiculous. I assure you that many mothers come to us as representatives of the people, telling us of their problems, saying: I should like to arrange to get rid of my children. I shall arrange with my cousin, my sister-in-law, my in-laws, to have them care for my children.
However mother-love still exists, Mr. Speaker, and the mother wants to keep in touch with her children. However, when it becomes financially impossible she sometimes has to consider such drastic solutions as parting with them, or at least pretending to do so as sometimes it is possible to place the children with the grandmother or grandfather and thus still maintain contact with them. But in such cases, the welfare service will move heaven and earth to oppose such a plan.
If there were an adequate children's allowance plan, such problems would be eliminated automatically, since mothers, parents with children they are unable to maintain decently because of an inadequate income would receive adequate allowances. This is why I find the principle is a good one but the amounts involved are inadequate.
Second, when one looks at this bill, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) put it so will, one finds it is all tangled up. I cannot get over how impossible it is to implement a bill such as this one without running continuously into problems begging description. One will understand that it is difficult to calculate income when because of the present economic instability the figures can change every week. One does not know exactly when a company will close down, thus creating unemployment. One does not know exactly when he will be a victim of the bad economic system, and even the position of those who presently have very adequate incomes is uncertain. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, the kind of trouble that can flow from the implementation of a bill such as the one before us.
I think universality always has this extraordinary advantage of guaranteeing a certain form of justice to all people. It will be said that it costs more, that it would be better to give more to those who need it and not to give to those who do not need it. Yes, Mr. Speaker, but there is an easy way to turn the difficulty. For example, why not make the benefits taxable? This way if we make those benefits taxable those who have incomes of $15,000, $20,000, $25,000 or $50,000 would have to add as income the amount of the benefits received in respect of their children and thus they would be simply paying back to the government those amounts which they received. As these amounts would be reimbursed, we could then increase them adequately and give the amount which is really needed rather than, once more, a kind of pittance, a small gratification on the eve of an election.

I think this impossible control, due to such legislation, should make us think. The minister should propose radical amendments in order to make this bill far more acceptable, especially if a distinction is going to be made to the effect that above a given income level, you do not need family allowances any more.
By making a distinction like this one, Mr. Speaker, what do we encourage? Once again, we encourage laziness, to a certain extent. In fact, we already face the problem of a certain class of people on welfare who, out of habit, and because of a wrong concept of our social legislation, would rather not work, not use their energy, not serve society, because it is easier to just sit back with your arms folded and your feet up on a case of beer and wait for time to go by.
Mr. Speaker, everybody deplores this system which results in the fact that in some municipalities, 30, 40, 50, or even 60 per cent of the people are on welfare. This is just encouraging laziness. I am not saying that those people are to blame; the system is.
When the government brings in a bill providing that from a certain level of income, the taxpayer is not entitled to family allowances, it is penalizing a worker whose energy and talents are normally used to increase the productivity of the country. The hard-working people are penalized, because they are resourceful, because they work, because they succeed with the wholesome ambition of receiving an adequate income.
This is another reason why the selective aspect of that plan is unacceptable.
I think that disregarding that indescribable chaos and impossible control, the government was concerned about one thing only-and that is regrettable-namely, the fact that it could tell the people that, from then on, family allowances would be $15 for children up to 12, and $20 up to 18. It seems that the purpose was, once more, window dressing, that is an increase which doubles or triples family allowances. This will look good but, in fact, what major change does this bring? We are still wondering.
Finally, in the analysis that I tried to make about this legislation, Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that I am very reluctant to accept it because of the constitutional difficulties arising from it.
Mr. Speaker, obviously, we will not be against the fact that amounts of money will be made available to Canadian families, but this will not keep me from stressing the extreme shortcomings of this bill. Why? Because this bill deals with a matter which, by virtue of the constitution and even plain common sense, should be totally controlled by the provinces. Mr. Speaker, family allowances were not instituted because during the war Quebec had a very weak government, and thanks to some special acts, the federal government could take over various provincial prerogatives. It took advantage of the situation to gain a foothold in a field which does not belong to it.
And why does it not? I said a while ago that it is a question of plain common sense. And why? Because, in a country as vast as Canada, although basic difficulties may
March 27, 1972

be the same, there may be as many ways of understanding them as there are regions.
It may be that in British Columbia people see social matters differently from the people in Quebec. That principle must be protected, Mr. Speaker. To my mind, we meddle again and increase constitutional difficulties every time we are asked to study a bill that trespasses on ground that should fall totally within provincial administration.
Recently we were informed about a so-called agreement between the federal government and the provincial government, based exclusively on correspondence between the two prime ministers. I wonder to what extent this might be the confirmation of the wishes of most Quebecers. However I wish to stress that this confirms an infringement that has already been made and which is extended by the application of this bill. That is in my opinion a very unfortunate situation.
They will say: That is once more a very particular opinion which does not reflect reality. But I would like to prove it by reading an editorial from the newspaper La Presse of Thursday, March 16, and I quote:
The former deputy minister for intergovernmental affairs in Quebec-
That is a man who has served under three different regimes in Quebec and who must know quite a bit about such things.
This is an agreement between the prime minister and a provincial premier and not between two governments. Here is what Mr. Morin has to say:
-if the "administrative compromise" proposed by Ottawa were accepted by Quebec and then sanctioned in constitutional legislation, the Province of Quebec would then formally recognize a right to which the federal government is not entitled in the field of allowances. Mr. Morin even voiced the opinion that mere agreement from the premier of Quebec to Ottawa's proposal would be sufficient, in the absence of constitutional legislation, to establish a precedent.
According to Mr. Morin, when all is said, there is more cause for concern than for celebration at the moment if the recent federal proposal is looked at closely. There is a danger that this proposal could annihilate all progress made by Quebec in the constitutional field and postpone for ever the basis of Quebec's claims, which is a true sharing of powers.
Mr. Speaker, this is what Quebec wants: an adequate and fair sharing of taxation powers. That is what Quebec wants. As for us, we advocate decentralization in that area so that each region of this country may be allowed to administer itself better.
How can the Minister of National Health and Welfare know here in Ottawa the particular problems of each province? If too much money is accumulated and if it is then necessary to infringe upon provincial jurisdiction to re-allocate the surplus, there is only one thing left to do: reduce taxes.
It is a mistake for the federal government to collect too many taxes, and because there is too much money, it is necessary to infringe upon provincial jurisdictions. This is a mistake and it is merely a matter of correcting it.
A short while ago, I was saying that it is very pleasing to exert a small control of sort over what closely affects individuals. That is why we won't drop what we have
Family Income Security Plan
already taken. Family allowances and old age security pensions should be administered by provinces; otherwise, we do not seem very responsible.
That is why in analyzing this bill, I must describe clearly the situation. As for Canadian taxpayers, no matter where the money comes from, they know that it eventually comes from their purses and therefore, no present is being made to them. So, they are ready to take it, whether it comes from federal, provincial or municipal governments. They are aware that this money belongs to them. Therefore, they will take it.
Taxpayers, of course, either from Quebec, from Manitoba, or from British Columbia, will take this money particularly as it belongs to them.
When I deal with the constitutional point of view, Mr. Speaker, I do not mean that Quebecers would refuse allowances for their children, but that in terms of administration, a mistake has been made and the federal government should have simply granted provinces the necessary fiscal authority to enable them to take these matters into their own hands. Those provinces which refuse are free to do so, but when one realizes that Quebec is ahead of the federal government in this respect, and that the programs are all set up and ready to be implemented were it not for lack of money, then, Mr. Speaker, I think that this question has been given little consideration and that sooner or later, we will regret it since a consensus has emerged to some degree among all Quebecers on this subject; we want constitutional reforms and a real sharing of responsibilities irrespective of the party we represent.
I believe that the bill before us is sanctioning an abnormal situation; there is no reason why an earlier precedent should be maintained. I think that the reform will have to be undertaken sooner or later.
Mr. Speaker, I now conclude my remarks. To round up my statement, I suggest that Canadians, whatever their province of origin, do not regard this as a gift but simply as a redistribution, though inadequate, of money taken from them. Why? Because it does not emanate from where it should. For example, the Quebec government has already established through its Department of Social Affairs, a comprehensive program in the social field. Having established a well coordinated over-all system, it should have material prosperity in order to apply it. This is what is called decentralization, so that each one can provide better administration.
Mr. Speaker, again, if we had a basic financial and economic system governed by logic, common sense and respect for the individual, the human being, such problems would be inexistent. We submit that we should guarantee to each Canadian a minimum income allowing him to live decently. Then, we would no longer need that impossible control over the meager allowances being handed out to families.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week when I was in my constituency, I was surprised to learn from a telephone call made to my office
1176

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
that the government had decided to re-introduce the family allowances bill, now known as Bill C-170. It was introduced on Friday for second reading. I wonder why. According to my information, the government was not to introduce it in until after the Easter recess. Some of my colleagues who spoke in this debate on Friday seemed to think that it was introduced Decause of the Newfoundland election. If that is so, Mr Speaker, the government did a pretty poor job of getting the message across, because, apart from the one telephone call to my office, I did not hear from one Newfoundlander who was aware of the facts. I, therefore, think my colleagues were wrong in assuming that the bill was introduced at this time because of the Newfoundland election. I think the bill was held in abeyance as a political manoeuver, and it was introduced on Friday because a federal election is going to be called right after the Easter recess. I repeat, the bill has been kept in abeyance as a political manoeuver, and has been so treated ever since the white paper on income security was introduced.
When I returned on Saturday, it was obvious from reading the local papers that not much attention was given to the bill. I hope this bill will finally be passed because it will increase the benefits to Canadian children up to and including the age of 17 years. I have tried to be reasonable in making representations to the government. I feel that my criticisms have been reasonable, at least that is my opinion. Also, I do not think I have been reluctant in giving credit to the government when credit was due.
I welcome the reintroduction of the family income security bill. However, I am sure no one in this House will blame me if I am suspicious of the government's intentions this time and about how far we will get with it. Apart from any political motives, I feel very strongly that increases in benefits to children of low income families must be implemented as quickly as possible. I believe this is an important step to ensure the proper growth of our future Canadian citizens and thereby ensure a better Canada. Also, it will help in some measure to alleviate poverty in this country.
Apart from some weaknesses pointed out by my colleagues, this bill is vitally necessary because over the years all governments have failed to provide enough opportunities for Canadians or to provide for the steady development of our human resources over the years, especially our youth. This program is vital because we failed to foresee the needs of the sixties and seventies by providing a well-planned program which would contain incentives to all Canadians, especially those with initiative. In the past we have failed to provide the poverty stricken adults of today with a well-planned program for education, decent health services, recreational services and all those things that were necessary for the development of our youth of yesterday. That is why we have one quarter of our population living below the poverty line today. That is why we have reached the stage in our society where we must deal with crisis after crisis by adopting helter-skelter programs to relieve poverty, sickness, disability, under-nourishment and suffering of so many of our citizens.
The real tragedy has come about because of our failure to recognize our poverty-stricken Canadians as human beings. We have failed to recognize that we are dealing with people. The government is so blinded by technological progress and trying to get answers to the problem of poverty by computers and studies by experts who were never poor that it forgets it should be concerned about people, not punchcards and computers. That is why we have a poverty rate of 25 per cent. One Canadian in four is a member of a family unit with an income that is below the poverty line. That is why 89 per cent of low income families in Canada are headed by persons who have not completed high school. Almost half of these did not complete elementary school. The reason is that governments failed in the past to foresee the need for education.
As a result of the blindness which results from reliance on the advice of sociological experts, the government has pushed citizens out of rural Canada into the cities by false inducements. As a result of this, 55 per cent of the low income families now live in urban areas. There has been a complete lack of concern for humans as a result of our past failures. The Senate committee report on poverty points out that 27 per cent of all heads of low income families are 65 years of age or over. The reason for this is that governments in the past failed to give the senior citizens leadership, opportunity and the basic necessities for life when they were young.
I think it is worthwhile to look at the events leading up to the introduction of Bill C-170 to show the devious strategy of the government in using various social programs for political purposes. The Throne Speech of 1968, the year this government came into power, outlined what the government was going to do for the poor. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that everyone in this country deserved equality of opportunity regardless of where he lived. He also said we must provide a decent livelihood for the poor of this country. The government then produced the famous white paper on income security. Without dealing with the dribbles given to the senior citizens and the war veterans, I want to deal with the section on family income security.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

It being five o'clock, the House now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, notices of motions and public bills.
