subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RESCINDING OF ORDER FOR DISCONTINUANCE OF RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of rescinding Order No. R.2673 of July 3, 1968 of the Canadian Transport Commission which gave authority to Canadian National Railways to discontinue rail passenger service in Newfoundland.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is almost 23 years to the day since Newfoundland became a province of Canada. It was on March 31, 1949, that the terms of Union between Newfoundland and Canada were consummated. During the negotiations leading up to the terms of union, a number of services operated by the then government of Newfoundland were, as a consequence of confederation, to come under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada. Allowance was made for the transfer of these services and utilities.
Included in the transfer was the Newfoundland Railway which was built at the turn of the century by the people of Newfoundland, at great expense and hardship, to open up the country. At that time it was a fully integrated rail service providing freight and passenger service, albeit a narrow gauge service. Term 31 of the Terms of Union between Newfoundland and Canada accordingly made provision for the transfer of these services from the government of Newfoundland to the government of Canada. Term 31 reads as follows:
At the date of Union, or as soon thereafter as practicable, Canada will take over the following services and will as from the date of Union relieve the Province of Newfoundland of the public costs incurred in respect of each service taken over, namely,
It goes on to list the services, the first being the Newfoundland rail service.
On July 3, 1968, the Canadian Transport Commission by its order R.2673 gave authority to the CNR to discontinue rail passenger service in Newfoundland. Since the summer of 1969, Newfoundland has been without rail passenger service, the only province so deprived. As a result, our province is suffering the consequences of a most inadequate system of public transportation. There are those who would argue-I shall not fall into this trap- that a legal case can be made out for asserting that the maintenance of the Newfoundland rail service is a responsibility which the government of Canada assumed in 1949 under the terms of union. It could be said that
Newfoundland Rail Passenger Service
according to a legal interpretation of term 31, and under the Order in Council which followed, whereby the government of Canada placed the Newfoundland rail service in the hands of the CNR for operation, the government of Canada had assumed an obligation under the constitution to continue operating this service-it was merely a formality for the government to ask its agent, Canadian National, to take on the responsibilities of actual operation.
Much has been said since that order was made on July 3, 1968 by Canadian Transport Commission. I think it bears repetition to say that this order was attained as a result of a series of events which can best be described as acts of collusion between the Canadian National, the Canadian Transport Commission, the Canadian government and the then government of Newfoundland. Canadian National deliberately set out to downgrade the service for whose maintenance they had assumed responsibility in 1949. I can only conclude this was done because the CN did not want to be bothered by having to order the special rolling stock required for a narrow gauge railway, in other words a railway which did not fit into its own system. In any event, they deliberately set out to downgrade the service to the point at which they could appear before the Transport Commission and make application for its discontinuance on the grounds that they were losing almost a million dollars a year. In actual fact, they were only able to show one year in which the operating loss amounted to $900,000. Even this was open to question because of the nature of the railways accounting practices, practices which, as is well known, are difficult to understand.
For example, the total cost of the operations of the stations and the support staff necessary to keep them operating is lumped in with the cost of operating the rail passenger service. In our view, 75 per cent of this cost should have been designated as being the responsibility of the freight service division. In other words, the rail passenger service accounted for only 25 per cent of the $900,000 deficit which the railway was able to show the Commission. At one time the then president of the CNR indicated there was a move on foot to change the railway's long-standing accounting practices. When officials of the company appear before the Transport Committee of this House I shall be interested to learn whether these practices have indeed been changed; they had not been changed up to last year.
Rail passenger service was replaced by a road cruiser service, which is a fancy name for a bus service. It is interesting to note that this bus service, notwithstanding the fact that it enjoys a monopoly in the province, is currently operating at an annual deficit amounting to almost half a million dollars. In my submission, this bus service is operating at a greater loss than the rail passenger service ever did. At best, the bus service is inadequate. There have been a total of 54 accidents to date, I believe. And there have been a number of unrecorded near-misses.
Another important factor to be considered is the considerable personal inconvenience suffered by the travelling public who are obliged to stand, in many cases without shelter, waiting for buses which, generally speaking, have difficulty in maintaining a schedule. Then, there is the
1178

travel cannot compete with other modes over long distances and through sparsely populated areas. This is why the Ministry of Transport and the CTC, at my direction, have stepped up their research in this important field ... It is by no means inconceivable that out of this combination of research and testing will come ideas and new designs which will make wholly new and more rapid and comfortable means of rail travel possible in many parts of Canada, including Newfoundland.
The minister knows better than I that you do not need advanced technology to provide an efficient rail passenger service in Newfoundland. All you need is a recognition by the railways of the constitutional right of the government of Canada to provide a rail passenger service in Newfoundland. Some direction from the government of Canada to Canadian National Railways to maintain the roadbed, which has been allowed to deteriorate, and to cut down some of the curves, is required. If this were done, then according to the evidence I have it would be possible for a passenger train to cross Newfoundland just as quickly, and certainly a great deal more safely, than a bus can at the present time, even the CN bus.
So, Mr. Speaker, the matter is a very simple one. Unfortunately, most of the rolling stock has been sold abroad. However, perhaps that is a blessing in disguise anyway because it was old and outdated and should be renewed. If the decision is made to restore the rail passenger service, then obviously new roiling stock will be required. It has been proven that cars operating on the mainland road beds of standard gauge can be carried quite efficiently on the narrow gauge used in Newfoundland. But the roadbed must be properly maintained.
I could go on, as I say, Mr. Speaker, but a number of my colleagues would like to join me in this debate. They feel just as strongly as, and in some cases even more strongly than, I do about this question. Therefore, may I conclude by saying that at the present time one of the radio stations in Newfoundland is operating a network program that has sponsored a petition to be sent to the government of Canada for the restoration of rail passenger service in the province. I am referring to the program "Phone Forum" broadcast from St. John's over radion station VOCM. Within the short time of two weeks the moderator of the program, Mr. Ron Pumphrey, tells me that he has received 12,000 names and expects shortly to see the total reach 25,000 names. When he gets a sufficient number of names, it is his intention to come to Ottawa to present this petition to the government of Canada. I believe that the majority of the people in Newfoundland support our contention that the rail passenger service in Newfoundland should be restored.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RESCINDING OF ORDER FOR DISCONTINUANCE OF RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate this afternoon I have no intention of trying in any way, shape or form to belittle the words of the previous speaker in respect of the discontinuance of railway passenger service in Newfoundland. As a member of the committee which conducted hearings on this matter, I travelled to Newfoundland to study the situation at first hand and I found it very interesting.
Like every member of this House, I come from a part of this country where the evolution of transportation is occurring. This evolution has been occurring literally for
Newfoundland Rail Passenger Service
years. We have all heard of the golden spike and we all know about the stagecoaches which made their final trips and were abandoned to storage in warehouses. There is a time for change in all types of transportation and we must give this fact serious consideration. Decisions must be made as to the future of various transportation systems. I submit decisions are being made in various parts of Canada in respect of the abandonment of rail service with which I do not agree. If I may digress for a moment, I should like to refer to a dangerous situation in the Fraser Canyon where an attempt is being made to discontinue part of this service. This matter will have to be given serious thought.
In perusing the information and evidence brought before the committee by many people, I found one or two points of particular concern. How many of these statements were made in an emotional vein and how many were made with a desire to keep the Newfoundland railway because of the use being made of it? It seems to me that the people of Newfoundland actually discontinued using the railway quite some time before the Canadian National Railways asked for permission to eliminate this service.
The last full year of rail passenger operation in Newfoundland was 1968, during which the total number of revenue passengers carried was 77,791. In 1969, the new CN road cruiser service was innovated. I agree with my hon. friend that this is perhaps a too fancy name for what is in fact a bus service. I say this because I have used this bus service in Newfoundland. In 1969 this service was implemented and carried 137,169 passengers. This increased in 1970 to 152,000 and in 1971 to 169,600.
There is a great deal of emotion involved in the abandonment of any traditional service. We all know about the old country stores in various areas, and I am not using that as a comparison here but rather as an example of how people cling to traditions because of emotion.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) stated there was a campaign under way in Newfoundland and that people were signing petitions. The figures he stated were very impressive, but I wonder whether the people who have signed these petitions will guarantee that they will use this service.
Amongst those who are charged with operating the various transportation systems across the country, there exists the saying in respect of these systems that you use them or lose them. I have been involved with aviation, and I know that many of the people who have signed petitions for certain services were not the people who used those services. I have a petition in my file now that I could use

March 27, 1972
Newfoundland Bail Passenger Service
as a case in point. The people who usually sign these petitions are those who want the other people to use the service.
I would be happy to support hon. members from Newfoundland in a request to the CNR to upgrade its road cruiser service. When the railway was constructed there was not a proper highway system. I would support hon. members in their effort to get better buses with better facilities, because I believe this would be more in line with the needs of Newfoundland. Newfoundland could make more use of the roads, both highway and secondary, if they were improved. I hope we can find sufficient moneys to make better roads available. This would improve the transportation services tremendously. Highways are very important to a transportation system which uses the vehicles available today. When considering priorities, I hope we will be more concerned about the construction of better highways and roads.
Let me make one point with reference to the suggestion that the Canadian government somehow failed to fulfil its obligation to Newfoundland because there was some guarantee the Newfoundland railway would continue forever and ever. That is not entirely true. Had the hon. member continued to read Term 31, he would have noted that the operative words are as follows:
-Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport, is pleased to order that, effective April 1, 1949, the Newfoundland Railway, including rights-of-way, wharves, dry docks and other real property, rolling stock, equipment, ships and other personal property- the title to which is vested in His Majesty, be and they are hereby entrusted in respect of management and operation thereof to the Company on the terms in the Canadian National Railways Act expressly specified, namely, that such management and operation shall continue during the pleasure of the Governor in Council-
I should like to emphasize the last phrase, "shall continue during the pleasure of the governor in council" . I have here a very interesting newspaper article which appeared in the Clarenville, Newfoundland, Packet. We are all members of parliament here, and because there is some indication that what I will read has a political tinge I would ask hon. members to take it into consideration. The article reads:
The editor of the Clarenville, Newfoundland, "Packet" says that there are five Newfoundlanders in Ottawa who are going to be pretty red-faced should the Progressive Conservative party win the next federal election.
The five are those remaining of the six Tories this province sent to represent us in Ottawa in the 1968 federal election. Their faces are going to be red because of their present insistence regarding the CN passenger trains in Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to pay tribute to the mover of this motion, the very eloquent hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). He and my colleagues from Newfoundland have been valiant and vigorous opponents of any diminution of transportation facilities in their province and his motion today is just a part of that continuing expression.
As a member from another province I want to lend my support to his advocacy. I come from a province which has also lost its rail passenger service. We do not even have service to the water's edge of the mainland. People who travel by train to P.E.I. now must derail at Amherst, Nova Scotia, and come the rest of the way by bus. If they have luggage that is heavier than they can take by hand, that is too bad. So we know some of the problems. The causeway approaches to the water's edge but not the railway. I think that the expression "use it or lose it" is not a very comprehensive analysis of the transportation situation in Canada. I am convinced that the plethora of abandonments of rail services in this country is an example of outrageous shortsightedness.
Also, I believe that the hon. member who moved this motion is correct, there is the juxtaposition of the developments: one is that the carrier diminishes the service in its quality, frequency and quantity, discourages the use of the common carfier by the citizens, by the potential patrons, and then when statistics build up to indicate that it does not have increasing use, that in fact it has decreasing use, it goes to the CTC and says, "Let us abandon it". This is exactly the problem. It is a built-in development toward extinction. I have here the latest report of the Canadian Transport Commission and it begins with a rationalization of the rail service. The rationalization of the rail service is full-fledged abandonment. should be realizing that the railways in this country do in fact have a future and, at the same time, the imaginative zeal which preceded the first railway age should be recreated and restored at the present time.
I read every day of rails being taken up and I predict that before many of us are dead they will be laying them again because in this mobile, fast moving era-and it will become more mobile and more rapid-the transportation of people and goods by rail is a great boon to our society. We know, Sir, that today we cannot build highways quickly enough. We know that cities all over this land, large, moderate and small, are having great problems with the automobile and with finding space. Many countries in the world, instead of discarding are upgrading their rail service and encouraging people to make use of it. I remember when many years ago the great moguls of the CNR came to Charlottetown and displayed at the Charlottetown railway station a museum car. I was saying that the government was introducing increased benefits for children all across Canada; the benefits were to be given according to family size and income; they were to be forthcoming in September, 1971, according to statements in the white paper. I must say, with due apologies to the poor people concerned, that the government had no intention of increasing benefits by that date. Its intention in that regard was about as great as the power of the poor people in this country to bring this measure about.
It is obvious now that this move was as calculated as anything could be. Whoever was commissioned to come up with the program should be ashamed of himself as a parent. The cabinet ministers responsible who decided on this strategy should be even more ashamed. I do not blame the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), Mr. Speaker, because I remember that about a year and a half ago a press release was issued which indicated that six cabinet ministers of this government had refused to go along with the recommendations of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Mr. Speaker, was their move not all too obvious when they decided that the proposals in the white paper did not fill the needs of Canadians? And those proposals were brought in as a result of the advice of experts.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we had the Willard report, the report of the deputy minister of national health and welfare. At the same time, a study was undertaken by the Senate Committee on Poverty. It was decided to give Senate committees something to do and that committee was established. It went across the country studying poverty again; not because they were interested in human beings who were suffering in Canada but because it was politically expedient to use tactics to delay bringing in a bill which would increase family allowance benefits.
What happened after that, Mr. Speaker? The government introduced Bill C-264 in the previous session and, according to the government's political strategy, increased benefits under that bill were promised for May 1, 1972. What did the government then do? It shelved the bill during the Christmas recess. At no time during the 16 months since the white paper on income security was introduced has the government been honest with Canadians about progress in the planning of this measure. At that time the bill was known as Bill C-264.

appears that there is to be another delay because of the Easter recess which is to come in a couple of days.

I said previously that I am willing to compromise for the good of the country, as is my party. I refer to the compromises between Quebec and Ottawa as contained in letters sent to the provincial premiers by the Prime Minister. According to the Prime Minister's letters to provincial premiers, the suggested system for family allowances would permit those provinces who wished to do so, to move toward an integrated system within their boundaries while maintaining certain general standards for poorer families. The federal government is willing to extend the principles involved to other income-support programs, and, if desired, a constitutional guarantee of the principles could be attempted in spite of the considerable difficulties that would be involved in making the generalized provisions necessary for a constitutional guarantee in an extremely complicated field.
The hope would be that such an arrangement would clean up the problem of social security to permit further progress in the process of constitutional review. The letters from the Prime Minister stated that the federal government would proceed with Bill C-170 in the current session and, after consultation with the provinces, would recommend to Parliament amendments to the bill at the appropriate stage.
Without going into the various inequities pointed out by experts on social legislation, the main failure of Bill C-170 is the lack of integration with other federal programs which are closely associated. An editorial in the Financial Times pointed out that the new family allowance legislation emphasises that the Minister of National Health and Welfare obviously never discusses anything with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to co-ordinate programs for the benefit of Canadians. For example, the adminis-

tration of the Family Income Security Plan is quite unrelated to the administration of other schemes such as unemployment insurance and income tax.
The Family Income Security Plan requires a new set of forms to be submitted to a special branch of the bureaucracy. Recent legislative changes have increased, but not consolidated the red tape and bureaucracy of income tax, unemployment insurance and now FISP. The principles of FISP are at odds with other social security schemes. For example, the government has opted for universality in medicare and unemployment insurance, but selectivity in FISP. Also, the "reformed" Income Tax Act has established uniform treatment for social benefits, but not FISP which allows tax free income.
Another example is that the Canada Assistance Plan contains a provision that, unless remedial action is taken before FISP is enacted, could undermine the object of the program to fight poverty. The problem is that under the Canada Assistance Plan the provinces are entitled to lower their rates of welfare assistance to families in proportion to the higher family allowance payments these families will be receiving.
Under clause 3(3)(b) there is provision that the provinces in determining the degree of need and arrangements for social assistance to applicants for welfare shall take into account all income maintenance payments through unemployment insurance, the Canada Pension Plan and guaranteed income supplement schemes. However, it is optional for the provinces to take into account family allowance and other schemes: this is a decision for the province to make. At the present time none of the provinces calculate family allowance payments as income for the purposes of social assistance; but it is possible they might, especially the hard pressed, poorer provinces. In all these ways the lack of integration of the FISP plan with other government programs and legislation means that the total package has a haphazard and sometimes contradictory effect.

For the same year, that is 1965-66, the amount spent by the Canadian government in servicing the debt reached $1,172 million; it will exceed two billion dollars this year. One can say without fear of erring that Canadian families have been sadly neglected.
With insufficient income, Canadians are going deeper into debt. Here is what La Presse reported on March 9, 1971, and I quote:
Canadians have sunk deeper into debt with banks, stores and finance companies by almost 5 per cent in 1970, and this increase in consumer credit occurred only during the last six months of the year ... compared to 1969, when the indebtedness increased by 14 per cent-
Secured personal loans, the most important group of loans, increased from $4.1 to $4.6 billion during the year-
Unsecured personal loans ... increased from $1 billion to $1.2 billion, while loans on insurance policies increased from $660 million to $745 million.
Therefore, consumer credit totalled approximately $11.3 billion in 1970.
Mr. Speaker, I shall quote from an article in the June 16, 1971, issue of La Presse, as follows:

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS

speechtext:
Debt is a rampant social evil in Quebec. It exceeds total government outlays of 4 billion dollars, and solely for consumer goods, according to a statement by Mr. Normand Caron of the Federation des associations d'economie familiale at the annual meeting of the Association cooperative feminine du Quebec.
The disasters, both individual and collective, it brings about are inconceivable, Mr. Caron stressed, claiming that the percentage of the family budget earmarked for payment of debts had increased from 8 per cent in 1955 to 28 per cent in 1969.
According to the lecturer, debts place the individual in a state of insecurity and tension and are often a cause of family disintegration because of conflicts they cause between husband and wife.
Mr. Speaker, insufficient incomes leave us with unsold products which are reflected in bad lodging conditions, poor clothing and many other services, including food consumption.
According to the Tuesday, November 11, 1969 issue of La Presse, milk consumption was decreasing in the province of Quebec while the government was penalizing farmers for producing too much.
In fact, at the convention held by the Quebec Industrial Milk Producers Association, National Council of Milk Producers Vice Chairman Jules Lafontaine stated and I quote:
Annual milk consumption in the province of Quebec has decreased by 100 pounds per capita compared with the level of 20 years ago.
In short, while farmers are being compelled by the government to reduce their production, it is being discovered that milk consumption is lower than the minimum suggested by the nutrition guide published by the government.

In my opinion, it would be in the interest of some departments to consult more often with one another.
It is obvious that the increase in family allowances is socially desirable. And among the 30 per cent of Canadians who live in poverty, there are many thousands of families with many dependents which deliberately, out of self-respect, have succeeded in living without the support of welfare. It is likely that a good number of those families lack the bare necessities and often have a lower family income than their neighbour who lives on welfare.
An increase in family allowances in my opinion would represent a valuable financial assistance, if I may refer to a newsletter published by the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce on the structures and output of the Canadian economy. It can even be asserted that despite the $150 million increase that is provided, Canadian heads of families will not buy more with these extra $150 million than they could buy in 1965.
Indeed, this quite significant table based on the value of the dollar in 1961 indicates that the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar which amounted to 93 cents in 1965 had decreased to 77 cents by 1970.
The consumer price index being set at 100 in 1961, the table shows that it went up to 107 in 1965 and reached 129 in 1970.
This means that in 1965, to purchase one dollar's worth of production, the Canadian dollar was worth 93 cents against only 77 cents in 1970.
As the figures which I have just given you were taken from a table published in 1970, I will quote once again an article which appeared in La Presse of May 12, 1971 and which was entitled: "The cost of living in Canada has risen by 33 per cent during a 10-year period." The following can then be read and I quote:
The cost of living for an average Canadian family has risen by about 33 per cent during a 10-year period.
Statistics Canada reports that the retail price index has gone up .7 per cent in April, largely due to raises for housing, clothes and food.
For each $100 spent in 1961 for goods and services, the consumer must now pay $132.20.
Mr. Speaker, these figures show that the Canadian dollar is now worth only 75 cents and that the $150 million suggested by the Minister of Natiortal Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) have no value whatever because of the rise in the cost of living and the dollar devaluation.
Another feature of the bill now before us is the selective system to be established, a system which will compell citizens to watch themselves, to evaluate themselves, and which will invite comparisons. The poor is compared with some one else who has succeeded in getting something. It will also force comparison between those who have attained a certain degree of success and those who have failed. It will provoke jealousy between those who give and those who receive.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, through the enforcement of such legislation, the government is simply going to distribute poverty. It simply wants to take money away from families which have too little as it is.
March 27, 1972

Thus, since a universal family allowance scheme is essential for maintaining the brotherly feelings within families as well as the community spirit among individuals, it would be in order, I think, to amend the bill now before us. It should be remembered that family allowances are not a salary but a right.
In times past, when production was insufficient because of famine, adverse conditions or floods and hurricanes, people necessarily had to resign themselves to the inevitable. They had to share among themselves since production was insufficient.
Since no one knows at the moment in Canada what to do with production, I am wondering why we are instituting a selective system for compulsory sharing. Production being sufficient, we are at liberty, as members of this House, to ask that our universal family allowance scheme be maintained.
In short, the universal scheme is maintained in respect of pensions paid to senior citizens of 65 and over. Consequently, in order to grant the same advantages to our younger people, it will be necessary that our economic life pattern undergo a transformation such that it will really be tantamount to a social organization. And I think that in order to reach this goal, many prejudices will have to be fought together with a host of selfish attitudes.
To change from the universal regime as we know it, to a selective plan will, I think, require the mobilization of thousands of people and I am convinced that the salaries paid to this new team of investigators will far exceed the total cost of a universal system.
The suggestion that a number of families can manage without family allowances is only valid, as we know, in respect of a minority of them in this country. We are also aware that the government is in a very good position, through its tax system, to fall back on those workers who receive too much. We know that very well.
Considering that we have already proposed in this House, the implementation of a guaranteed income scheme, which is inevitable in the long run, I think we should take the opportunity to implement part of this project. Whatever the salaries earned by parents, the government should normally co-operate with them through universal aid measures that will guarantee the well being of dependent children. I believe that these allowances should be scaled in such a way as to represent a substantial contribution toward the child's care and should also take into account the expenses incurred for older children. It is only necessary that we establish for our younger people a system covering the basic needs of food, clothing and shelter. This minimum is absolutely attainable given the present economic conditions of our country.
Mr. Speaker, if the young of today are tomorrow's generation, they are as much the heirs of those which have preceeded them.
And the answer in respect of the family allowances scheme comes quite simply from the fact that any person is entitled to something, by the mere fact of being born. Since family allowances are not considered as a supplement to the salary or income of the family head, the funds used to pay them should not be levied through a tax on the income of working people.
Family Income Security Plan
Family allowances are not earned income but a social measure designed to provide an equitable income for the families of workers and to remedy inequities in the present economic system. Those measures which guarantee social security are born of the commendable desire to relieve economic distress and to acknowledge the right of the children of this country to have their basic needs met.
The newborn child or the child who is growing up do not take part in the production of goods which are given to them freely. However, we acknowledge their right to a share of the riches produced. From the mere fact of being born, they are entitled to satisfaction of their basic needs. And those allowances should come not from the result of the labour of those who work in order to make a living, but only from the social fund built through the social factors of production, through the work of machines, in whose inheritance we all share.
There is more to it than that, Mr. Speaker. Since those social revenues are the result of education, of the centuries old work of machines, and of the development of techniques, there should be no discrimination in the distribution of social production. The right to social products should not be limited to only a few children in the country, because no matter what family they live in they are entitled to the things they need in order to sustain and develop their lives.
In order for the new measure to benefit the whole population, its implementation should be related to the establishment of new credits. We find that the gap between total purchasing power of Canadians and national output is growing wider from day to day.
In 1961, for example, the gross national product was $39 billion while national income stood at $29 billion. In 1971, the GNP was $95 billion while national income barely reached $70 billion. I think this difference of $25 billion is enough for us to suggest the creation of money which could be paid out to all family heads of this country. I think that before telling us it is impossible we could try it for a year. The government is making all kinds of experiments. Recently a hovercraft that will probably never hover was built. Planes that will probably never fly were built and discarded.
So, I think it is within that frame of mind that we should be proceding with this experiment of using new credit. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, if tne government can afford to spend on experiments with doubtful results, surely it could afford to make an experiment which we are convinced will end up benefiting all Canadian families.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I never thought that I would be standing in my place in defence of something Mackenzie King did, but for once I am going publicly to support a measure brought in by that meandering person whom we had for so many years as prime minister of this country. When he brought into being the family allowance scheme in 1944, he acknowledged the need in our social security system for special recognition that married couples with children face circumstances and requirements which warrant income provision during the time their children are living at home. He was socially sound in his judgment that such

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
schemes should be brought in on a universal basis. I cannot emphasize too much the significant social relevance of having such schemes on a universal basis.
What is fundamentally involved here apart from the dollar value of the current legislation-I shall come to that in a few moments-is the principle involved in having a piece of government legislation which is doing a complete about-face in terms of its commitment of 1944 on the question of universality in social legislation: its consequences for the future well-being in particular of the category of poor family about which the government proclaims it is most concerned cannot be over-emphasized.
I wish to make three points about this legislation which bear in one way or another directly on this issue. It seems to me that by introducing the discriminatory income position basis of the family into the eligibility criteria for family allowances we are making a great mistake, a decisive about-turn in the history of social legislation in Canada. The first point, which I believe is very important, to be made on this question is that it is a socially divisive act. There can be no doubt that in the future families-I do not say this applies to all families, but to many families in most communities-will regard each other in terms of whether or not they are eligible for family allowance, exactly analogous to the way in which families now regard one another in terms of their eligibility for welfare assistance. That is exactly what the government is doing. It is proposing a measure in terms of social consequences or assistance to the family which puts family allowances on a welfare assistance basis. Some government members may deny this. I see some shaking their heads. That is precisely the consequence of the legislation. The legislation is saying to the people of Canada that if their income position is such and such vis-a-vis the number of children they have, then they may receive the family allowance. It is saying that if they do not meet the criteria, they will not receive it.
Therefore, this legislation is saying that we recognize in the form of our social insurance provisions those who have and those who have not. We are stratifying the population of Canada in terms of this age-old distinction. We are doing it in a way which was not the case under the original family allowance legislation. One of its most significant social graces was the fact that it did not discriminate among Canadians.
Apart from the negative effect this kind of division will have on adults in terms of their perception of themselves and the self-perception of their children, it will involve an act of discrimination on the basis of income between those who will receive it and those who will not. It is this, I predict, which will serve to undermine the future actions of this or any other government in attempts to provide improved benefits which are necessary for the poor in our society.
I want to state as precisely as I can my reason for believing this. I repeat that I regard this question as being of profound importance. If my judgment is right it will have a profound consequence, and if I am wrong it will not. It is a matter of judgment. What we are doing in Canada now is this: we are saying to the working people 
they are to be divided into categories. I am thinking now on the one hand of reasonably well-off workers, in which category I would place most workers who are organized in the trade union movement as well as a number of others, and on the other the working poor.
In effect, we are saying to those at the upper income level of working people that at some point they will not receive family allowance benefits. We are saying to the organized lumber workers, the packinghouse workers, the steelworkers, the auto workers and reasonably well paid people in offices, as well as elementary and high school teachers in Canada, that they are not to receive family allowances any longer. They will not receive the benefits but will have to pay for those who will. This is the social point.
It seems to me that for the first time in the history of this country, in terms of social legislation, we are about to take a decisive backward step in which people are to be asked to pay increased amounts for benefits for which they will be ineligible although they are benefits which should accrue, and have accrued previously, to all. In future years this will undermine the willingness of this category of worker to continue to pay for benefits which other people will need and will receive. I think that is the important issue here.
Up to the present we have had the support of teachers, fishermen and other organized workers in respect of extensions and improvements in the social insurance system, whether on the basis of old age security or family allowance. We had their support because they would receive benefit. As members of the community, they were being asked to pay for the well being of others and for something from which they also would enjoy some benefit. In the present legislation, by restricting the number of recipient families, however, we have taken a step which will undermine the willingness of a substantial portion of our population to continue to contribute to badly needed improvements in social services for the community.
So the government-I will come to the dollars and cents implications in a minute-in their argument that they are really providing substantial benefits for those with the lowest incomes, those who need it most in terms of the long run, and by long run I mean beginning a year or two from now, are really undermining their own position because they are working against the kind of political support that is needed in any kind of community to sustain social welfare.
Whether it is in a democracy in Canada, the United States or Scandinavia, for the vast majority of the community to support social insurance schemes they themselves must see a direct benefit to themselves. There is nothing selfish in that; it is very much a part of human psychology. You cannot expect a total giving to someone else when you get nothing in return. I think that principle of universal community benefit is in jeopardy here. We are therefore building up a potential political opposition in Canada to continuing improvements in our social insurance schemes.
The second point I should like to make is that in terms of implementing this scheme every family in Canada will
March 27, 1972

need its own little computer. Every politician in this House of Commons, or the ones who remain after the forthcoming general election, will I predict be confronted by irate citizens who think they are either entitled to receive the family allowance in principle or that they should receive it at a certain higher level. The politicians will be inundated with demands for changes, with demands to remove bureaucratic delays.
I predict that the bureaucratic foul-up that we have seen with the unemployment insurance regulations will seem like a tea party in comparison with what we will see when the family allowance legislation takes effect next fall. To repeat the point, any average citizen who spends most of his time working will need some kind of computer to make sense of the scheme with any degree of rapidity. One of the virtues of good legislation is that it can be readily understood by a non-expert. This is precisely what this legislation fails to achieve.

speechtext: Wait until we see the regulations.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member is absolutely correct. Both he and I were on the committee that dealt with unemployment insurance and we saw the morass that came from that legislation in terms of its detailed regulations. This government prides itself so often on its business efficiency. The cost argument alone in implementing this piece of legislation should have perhaps been sufficient for not supporting it. It will be a complicated bureaucratic mess.
The third point that I should like to make bears directly on the dollars and cents issue. It is that the legislation introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) when considered, as it should be, as part of a total package of the financial measures introduced by this government with the tax bill that we discussed in the House last week, is seen not to benefit the poor in its cumulative effect nearly as much as it benefits the rich. It will be recalled that the minister and other supporters of the family allowance legislation have suggested that they are taking the money back from the rich who really do not need it. They ask us what we who are talking about the need for genuine social improvement are really complaining about. May I remind the House that if we consider the tax legislation that was introduced last week, it is the rich in Canada who are really going to benefit from the acts of this government.
I need not remind hon. members that it is quite plausible for us to expect an election this year. In 1972, what the government is taking away from the rich in the family allowance scheme, it is more than giving back with concessions in income tax. If we add the two together, the tax benefit plus the family allowance benefit, and consider who benefits most from the actions of this government in the past ten days, it will be clearly seen that richer Canadians come out on top.
I have before me a table which compares these benefits for a family with two children. Assuming that the family allowance legislation is passed-as it will be, with a government majority-and comes into effect next September 1, we discover that for 1972 a family with two children whose total income is $3,000 will have a total benefit of $216. We find that a family earning $4,000 will have a

benefit of	$218.19;	a	family	earning	$5,000	will	have	abenefit of	$225.06;	a	family	earning	$6,000	will	have	abenefit of	$206.19;	a	family	earning	$7,000	will	have	abenefit of	$187.68;	a	family	earning	$8,000	will	have	a

When we go up to a family whose income is $11,000, we begin to see an interesting development, namely, a substantial improvement in the net benefit coming from the government from these two pieces of legislation. Let us consider a family earning $20,000. We find that under the proposed scheme, in family allowance plus tax benefits in terms of the tax reduction that was given by this government in the legislation that we debated last week, the family earning $20,000 will save $260.58; a man earning $25,000 will save $328.83; a man earning $30,000 will save $400,68; a man earning $50,000 will save $716.25; and a man earning $75,000 will save $1,153.14. A man who is eking out an existence and is able to afford only two or three trips round the world, who makes $100,000 a year, due to the generosity of this government which is so overwhelmingly concerned with the problems of the poor will save $1,611.39!

speechtext: The rich get rich and the poor get children.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
The conclusion seems rather obvious. The rich, if we define them for our purposes here as those who are earning $15,000 and more, will get more in net benefits from these two pieces of legislation in 1972 than will the poor-if we define the poor for purposes of our discussion as those earning from $3,000 up to and including $8,000. The other point to be made is that those in the middle-income range, those earning between $10,000 and $15,000, will be gaining less than the poor, which is understandable, and will also be gaining less than the rich, if we define the rich as those earning more than $15,000 a year.
To go back to the point I made very early in my remarks, it is that middle-income category of people who are very important in terms of maintaining their support for significant improvement in social insurance legislation, whether in respect of family allowances or anything else. It is this category of men and women who in the main are working very hard. These are the people earning between $10,000 and $15,000 who will feel the negative effects of this family allowance legislation and who will not benefit to any great degree from tax reductions. Consequently, these people will be increasingly reluctant to support significant improvements in social services proposed by this government by a provincial government or by government at any level.
The government expects to count on this category of income earners for support in the coming election. To be frank, Mr. Speaker, they are the kind of people who tended to support the government in the past. But their support is being whittled away precisely because the gov-

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
ernment is beginning to exclude them from the benefits that accrue from good social insurance legislation.
I would like to conclude by saying that in spite of the benefits that this legislation will provide for the poor, it completely undermines the universality aspect of social insurance legislation in Canada. It is a retrograde step, the first of its kind in Canadian history in this area, and therefore does not warrant support. Its benefits could be much more effectively provided by significant reform in taxation. I will not take the time of the House to go into this matter; I have spoken on it in the past as have other hon. members of my party. We believe the needs of the poor should be looked after by significant tax reform.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer a few suggestions with respect to Bill C-170. Like the hon. member who preceded me, I believe that the government, in not opting to have the family allowance included in an individual's income, has made the administration of the plan much more difficult without really achieving what it set out to do, to provide something of greater value to the low-income family. It has been said many times by many people that the dollar value of a family's income is a poor measurement of how the family is able to live in our society. Nevertheless, I have to accept that the use of the income tax method is the only way in which measurement can be made of a family's income but it is only a rough method of assessing the social standard of living of any family.
For instance, in Manitoba we have always been told by the people who live in the north of the province that they should have an increased income tax exemption because of the increased cost of living in that area. It has often been said that north of 53 degrees in Manitoba each family should have an additional $1,000 a year exemption. When one has personal experience of the area, one must agree that there is much to be said for that point of view.
In a program such as this, Mr. Speaker, where a specific dollar value can be paid to every child or youth through guardians or parents it seems most likely that universality should be inherent in the plan. In order to preserve the idea that low-income families should benefit the most, it seems to me that by adding the family allowance to income and taking the normal percentage of income tax that can be deducted all Canadian citizens should have a better and fairer return with respect to their income. If we decide that further relief should be given to our lower income groups, we could do this by means of a tax cut or by a change in the income tax rate benefiting those at the lower income level who need it most. It seems to me that the method proposed by this bill whereby applications for benefit will have to be filed along with an estimate of family income is an unnecessarily cumbersome method of arriving at the figure that the benefit should be in each case.
The bill provides that families are allowed to file a revised estimate of income at intervals of four months should their financial status change, and benefits would then be adjusted. Initially, families will be allowed to file estimates of income based on last year's earnings or on earnings projected for next year, whichever is most favourable to them. I cannot imagine a more complicated system. In most cases the responsibility will fall, as usual,

on the woman of the household to make the application even though she may not always know whether her husband has had an increase or decrease in income.
Then there are families, and here I speak of farmers, whose income is averaged over a five-year period. There are self-employed people whose income may vary from nothing in one year to many thousands of dollars in another. All this will create a great administrative problem and I am afraid will mean considerable variance in the benfits, particularly those paid to people whose incomes fluctuate each year. There is no doubt that widespread administrative inequities will occur under this complicated system. It seems logical that had the universality of the program been continued, with the benefit added to family income, the money could have been just as effectively used to aid low-income groups and could have been just as effectively distributed to those who need it most.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, if we give the basic old age pension to every citizen who reaches a certain age, we should also give a basic income to all our new citizens who have not yet entered the economy. I believe this bill is unnecessarily complicated and will require frequent amendment. It leaves itself open to administrative problems and considerable inequities in the calculation of payment of benefits. As has been outlined by other hon. members, when the regulations are introduced they will further increase the problems of members of parliament trying to resolve the difficulties connected with this program.
I would like to speak for a moment on the value of programs such as this in respect of the alleviation of poverty. It seems to me that when a program such as this is introduced there is an immediate benefit in redistributing income but as time passes this benefit decreases. It seems to be decreased because segments of society, high wage earners and entrepreneurs, those who are the bellwethers of society, are in a position to demand and receive higher incomes so that their take-home pay remains at a level comparable to what it was before the advent of the program. In other words, our economic system and tax structure seem to adjust themselves so that the members of our society who lose money in taxation to provide these benefits are able to recoup their losses by means of wage settlements and imposing higher prices for goods. Perhaps this is part of the general inflationary trend.
Perhaps for these reason it is generally considered that family allowance plans have had no great value in fighting poverty. Often these plans have to be analysed to see how they fit in with the original program. The data as to the effect of family allowances on combating poverty seems to be equivocal and can be construed in many different ways. While the poor pay relatively little in direct income tax to our treasury, in the form of indirect taxes a major burden is imposed on the poor.
The Croll report, the report of the Senate Committee on Poverty, cited figures from 1961 to show that 56.5 per cent of the income of those earning less than $2,000, before transfer payments, goes in taxes and of this 56.5 per cent
March 27, 1972

only slightly more than 1 per cent is taken directly in individual income tax. The dilemma of increasing income tax is that eventually, unless some money is left to the individual taxpayer, he presumably will not be a member of the labour force or productive in any manner other than through dollar value. Fighting poverty with the family allowance probably is not as rewarding as people would wish.
Mr. Speaker, I should not end these comments without a few words on what is being discussed the world over, and that is the mood that is prevalent, namely, that if man is to stay on this planet we may have to approach a zero population growth. The comment of the President of the United States last week regarding population growth has given events a new turn. The comment urged the United States to welcome a plan for stabilized population. On March 13, 1972, an article in the Globe and Mail commented:
A government-appointed panel Saturday proposed that the United States try to halt the rise in population and "enable individuals to avoid unwanted childbearing".
"We have looked for, an have not found any convincing economic argument for continued national population growth," John D. Rockefeller, chairman of the commission on population growth and the American future, said.
Mr. Rockefeller told a press conference he believed the United States would be the first country to adopt a population policy aimed at ending growth, if it accepted the panel's proposals.
The panel said that even if the birthrate maintained its downward trend to the point where married couples had an average of only two children, the U.S. population would continue to grow for nearly 70 years. This is because so many now are of child-producing age.
There has been considerable discussion as to whether the family allowance program increases the tendency to larger populations. It has been considered, and studies have shown conclusively, that family allowances are not an incentive to an increasing birthrate. But at an international conference on children's allowances in 1968 the participants gave evidence that there is no direct relation between the existence or characteristics of a children's allowance system and the birthrate. This is perhaps, in the over-all view, quite right, but in the lower income segments of some groups there has been in the past a tendency to increase the family income by prolific birthrate. However, once these groups attain their material desires there seems to be a tendency for a fall-off in the birthrate.
There are those who advocate reduced payments to larger families as a disincentive to a high birthrate. This is not generally accepted yet, but I think that at some time in the future, and not too far away, more thought will be given to it. In any case, the role of the family allowance as a stimulus to the birthrate does not seem to be very strong.
In this legislation the government has departed from universality. It has increased the problems of administration and cost and will create many social inequities that could have been avoided merely by adding the income from family supplement to family income and taxing it at the usual rate.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for recognizing me. For a moment I thought I was not to have the opportunity of participating in the
Family Income Security Plan
discussion on this significant piece of legislation. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) is in his place on the other side of the chamber. I did not hear what he said, but I am sure it was worth while. He can be a nice fellow at times, but I wonder what he thinks of this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder what happened to the participatory democracy that this government was supposed to bring forth and which would give Canadians an opportunity to put before this House of Commons their ideas on where our country should go in terms of social welfare policy? I am very disturbed to find that there is a trend-

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: A pernicious trend.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
-a pernicious trend that seems to be projected by this government. We had a white paper on the tax bill. Thank goodness that was referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs so that we had an opportunity of ascertaining the direction we should take with respect to tax reform. Many worth-while suggestions came from that committee and as a result we have a better-although imperfect, if you will, Mr. Speaker-bill. We on this side of the House would never say it is perfect, but many of the inequities that were pointed out by members of the opposition made it possible for the bill to become more acceptable.
On November 30, 1970, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) issued his white paper on income security for Canadians. I was under the impression, as were many hon. members, that this document would be placed before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs following the pattern that had been decided upon by this government, thereby giving the many Canadians involved an opportunity for their voices to be heard. In answer to a question which I posed this afternoon, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the great exponent of the just society and participatory democracy, indicated that with respect to the proposed airport in the township of Pickering he, in a unilateral way and under the British North America Act, had come upon a solution. As far as he was concerned, if 51 per cent of the people affected-I do not know how he could ever determine that-did not want the airport, there would not be one. I am not questioning whether there is going to be an airport. I am trying to point out that there is a fraudulent aspect to this government's conception of participatory democracy.

speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member should address the Chair.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. I was saying that someone has to speak for the middle-income man who, it seems to me, is being ignored. He is the only one who sees himself. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) dwelt on this question. It is time we started to give the man in this group some incentives, not disincentives. It seems that every piece of legislation is directed toward him adversely. I wonder how many lumps he can stand. Hon. members know what the Prime Minister said with regard to lumps: he said if they don't like it, they can lump it.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: When did he say that?

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
I hear the Minister of Agriculture. The Prime Minister said it and he meant it. Hopefully, a lot of people will take him at his word and let him know how many lumps they can stand. All I ask is how many lumps the middle man can stand. His land taxes are going up; he is paying a greater chunk as a result of the white paper on tax reform; he is being emasculated in terms of whatever contribution he receives from this government.
As far as I am concerned, one and a half million people will not be covered by this plan. If this is the type of just society we have to live in, it is not fair. A man is prepared to stand up and be his brother's keeper, but there always comes a time when he has to think about himself and his family. He will find that the government does not have a heart, compassion or the understanding that he who pays the shot must be recognized at some time. If the government does not get that message I have no hesitation or reservation in stating that the polls will let them know how many lumps these people can take.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Another thing that bothers me about this act is its complexity. I would not even attempt to explain to anyone in this House how an individual will get his money or how much he will get. If you think the Unemployment Insurance Act was beyond immediate comprehension, wait until you get into this act! What concerns me about this bill, and I say this with a great deal of respect, is that it is being directed toward people who perhaps are not adequately prepared to complete the forms that are necessary for this measure to come to fruition.
Are we building up a bureaucratic society second to none? It is amazing. Do you know how much we now spend? We spend $16 billion a year. Without having looked into this too deeply, I say that a lot of it goes into unnecessary bureaucratic administration. This comes through acts which are imperfect and complicated such as the Unemployment Insurance Act and this one.

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
You sound like an old Tory.

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Whose voice was that? Was it the member for Windsor. There is one thing about him, his voice is loud; it carries.
I get back to my point. There is something about this bill which disturbs me. We who are involved with the standing committee will have to look into this matter very profoundly, because mistakes have been made in the Opportunities for Youth program and LIP. I am not going to talk about the merits of those programs; that can be done at another time. I am talking about the forms that will have to be completed in order to be able to take advantage of this program. My experience leads me to believe that they will follow the same pattern as forms for the Opportunities for Youth and LIP. There will be a lot of frustrated people whom we should be helping. I do not know where the forms will come from; perhaps the regulations. In order for people to be in a position to take advantage of this scheme we must ensure that the forms are as simple as possible. The type of person who will be taking advantage of this program does not have the capacity to complete complicated forms.
I have looked at some of the forms required under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not claim to be very clever, but with my training I should have a sufficient awareness of how to fill out forms. With all respect, I find them highly complex. As a matter of fact, they are so complex it will lead people to frustration and lateness in filing. They are embarrassed because they do not know how to complete the forms. If they do complete them, they are wrong. Even though the government has an idea, I hope the forms they bring out will be understandable, concise and relatively easy to complete. In this way we will be helping people, not throwing forms at them which they cannot understand.
I want to move into other areas. I read an editorial in the September 20, 1971, edition of the Financial Times with regard to the proposed new legislation. I quote:
The new legislation on family allowances which Mr. John Munro presented to Parliament last week is a dreadful example of the incoherent muddling which is emerging as the hallmark of the Trudeau government.
Those are not my words. I am not trying to be nasty; I am just trying to agree. I am reading into the record-

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: Isn't that the Prime Minister's authority?

maintopic: TWENTY-EIGHT PER CENT OF FAMILY BUDGET FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Perhaps you are right. I quote further:
There is little evidence there that Mr. Munro discusses anything with Mr. Mackasey or that either of them speaks to Mr. Benson. If any ministers are in communication with God, that remains a private matter: obviously they do not get the same answers.
I notice that the hon. member for Windsor laughs. This is true: the truth of this criticism can be proven in several ways. I will go through them; I will touch upon them in a significant way. I want to be concrete and concise. The principles of FISP are at odds with other social security schemes. The government has opted for universality in medicare and unemployment insurance, but selectivity in FISP. Also, the "reformed" Income Tax Act has established uniform treatment for social benefits except for FISP, which gives tax-free income.
I will touch on administration. The administration of FISP is quite unrelated to the administration of other
(Mr. Olson.]
schemes such as unemployment insurance and income tax. FISP requires a brand new set of forms to be submitted to a separate branch of bureaucracy. Recent legislative changes have therefore increased but have not been consolidated, as I pointed out earlier. I refer to the red tape and bureaucracy of income tax, unemployment insurance and now FISP programs.
Let me touch on another group which I believe is of some significance, namely, working wives. The new tax reform legislation includes deductions and measures, however imperfect, to compensate working wives for daycare costs for their children. The new Unemployment Insurance Act provides maternity benefits to be paid to pregnant women while they are away from work to have children. In contrast to these positive steps to recognize the costs of having children and to provide an incentive for remaining at a job, FISP takes a negative step: FISP penalizes working wives through its cut-off levels being based on gross family income.
Let me give an illustration. If a wife goes to work to supplement her husband's meagre salary, it is quite likely that her added income will push total family income above the cut-off level and she will therefore forfeit part or all of her family allowance cheques. For a middle-class wife this effect may not be too important, but for a family struggling to get out of poverty the loss of even a baby bonus cheque hurts. Consequently, FISP has a built-in disincentive.
This is what we on this side of the House are always talking about. It does not seem to reach the other side. We always talk about incentives. This government continually implements disincentives. I repeat, consequently FISP has a built-in disincentive for working mothers who know that they will probably lose part or all their family allowance cheque as a result.
Cut-off levels should be based on net income after deductions, rather than on gross income. This would be more meaningful. In this way personal income tax exemptions and child-care deductions will have their full power for working wives. Benefit cut-off levels could then be scaled to ensure that poverty-stricken families benefit most from family allowances. When I start to think about the cut-off levels I wonder why $4,500 was picked as the minimum and $9,100 as the maximum, the least deserving of any level.
There is an inconsistency among government departments in their assessment of when families need government support. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) takes into account the fact that it costs more to raise a child once he reached the age of 12 years, whereas the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his new Income Tax Act did not recognize that children cost more to raise until they reach the age of 16. This is why I wonder what is going on here. Do we ever discuss where, why and how we are going?
It seems that one minister contradicts another. As I said, the Minister of National Health and Welfare believes that a family with one child and a gross income of $4,500 or less should get maximum assistance from his department. The unfortunate thing about the white paper and the new tax bill is that through the Department of Finance a substantial tax continues to be imposed on the
March 27, 1972

same person. How can we rationalize that when on one hand the Minister of National Health and Welfare says that if you earn $4,500 and have one child, you are entitled to full benefits, and on the other hand the Minister of Finance says that he will not go along with that and will tax and take all he can get? I think I have placed some points before the House for serious consideration.
We have to reward initiative. I repeat that those who have been paying the shot for so long should be rewarded now and again. As it is, it seems the only time they will ever get anything is when they reach the age of 65. When they are 65 they will get old age security benefits and, maybe, benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. Otherwise there do not seem to be any programs of which they can take advantage so that they may project themselves into the good life and feel happy about it.
This is why I say: Be careful: Do not go too far, continually taking from so many people while at the same time leaving initiative without reward. Such a policy is bound to backfire. As I walk around my riding and talk to the people with whom I am concerned and who are concerned with me, I find there is a feeling permeating society and reflected in my riding, that we had better start rewarding initiative. Otherwise, why should a person continue to break his back? Can members opposite give me one good reason why anyone should continue to break his back to pay taxes when he finds that at times his money is spent in a haphazard, irresponsible way or even squandered?
At the same time, the people I am talking about can never seem to get a loan or a subsidy. All they seem to get are tax bills. Come April 30 they will start getting demands saying: You owe us so much. At least if you do not pay you are not sent to jail. I know this because I have been delinquent: I still am, as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker. But there are no concessions except that the authorities will take it easy and charge interest at 5 per cent.
I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is in the chamber, a friend of mine from Hamilton, so I will repeat a few of the remarks I have made. I hope, in any case, he will read my speech in Hansard tomorrow. It was not a very significant speech but it was one given in all sincerity. I have tried to outline a few areas of concern. I know the minister of health understands what I am talking about when I say we ought to reward initiative. I am repeating myself, but the minister was not here and I want to bring this to his attention. We cannot go on creating disincentives which affect the man who is paying the shot. We have to show some interest in him.
I have another point with respect to the regulations. I find that the regulations which people are asked to follow up by way of forms are too complex to be understood by those we are trying to reach. I hope that the minister in his charity-he is a charitable fellow-will do something to see that these forms are made easier to fill out by those we are trying to reach.
Let me close by saying once again that if ever this country is to move toward an economy in which everyone can enjoy equal opportunity, including opportunities for employment-and I believe we all want to work; I do not accept that there is a right not to work; I do not think we
Family Income Security Plan
are yet ready for that-it is necessary to create a climate in which the economy can develop and move into an era of profound economic growth leading to greater productivity and, hence, to full employment. Then there will be no need of provisions such as we are considering at the moment.
