speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is about four years since I heard the maiden speech of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). I shall never forget that speech because in it he set forth his philosophy of life. In essence, he said:
Judge not a man by the colour of his skin,	.
Or the way he looks or fights or sins,
Or the gods he serves or the wine he drinks,
But judge a man by the way he thinks.
Tonight we heard that philosophy reiterated by the hon. member. He spoke with clarity and conciseness and he certainly convinced many of us on this side with regard to the points he put forward. I could add an addendum to that by saying that if an NDP member is not elected during the next election in Hamilton West, then I hope the present member is re-elected.
On November 30, 1970, the government tabled its white paper on income security for Canadians. The purport of that report covered two main subjects. One concerned the treatment of pensions for senior citizens and the second covered family allowances. Many of us were prepared to forgive the minister at that time for not sending the white paper to the committee for study in depth, because in the month of December, 1970, the government introduced its old age security legislation. Well do we remember the matters contained in that legislation in 1970, and more especially the 42 cents increase given our pensioners, right at Christmas time. Not only did the government make a generous increase of 42 cents, but it froze the cost of living clause at 2 per cent for those who were going to receive the $80.
That was the first benefit received by our senior citizens from the white paper on income security for Canadians. Many of us were very unhappy about this because at that time the minister was introducing a principle to which many of us are strongly opposed, namely, the principle of selectivity as opposed to that of universality. I am sure that if Mackenzie King were here tonight-and he may be in spirit-he would recall the legislation for which he was responsible in 1944 which introduced for the first time in the history of Canadian social welfare the principle of universality. He or his spirit would shed buckets of tears at what the government he once led has now done to the principle of universality.
Not only has the minister dropped this principle from the old age security legislation but he is now attempting through Bill C-170 once more to drop the principle of universality in favour of selectivity in the field of family allowances. I am rather amazed that the minister would introduce such a principle. He comes from the city of Hamilton, a city composed of working people with a wide scale of income. The minister is now adopting the principle that payment of family allowance shall be determined

March 27, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
by family income. It is, in effect, a polarization of income which determines whether or not a person is entitled to family allowance.
Although we have polarization taking place in other parts of the world, now is not the time to introduce this principle in Canada. In fact, the government has been strongly opposed to polarization in many fields, such as the different nationalities within our country, the cultural rights of the people and also linguistic rights. Many of us on this side have not been very proud of the government in this respect. We do not think that polarization of nationalities, culture and language should be allowed to take place. Yet while the government adopts this principle of polarization it rejects the principle of universality in the payment of family allowances, and I suggest that such rejection is not worthy of support.
Some of our speakers have indicated the results that will flow from this type of legislation. When the legislation giving the 42 cents increase to our pensioners was passed in December, 1970, as well as the legislation that gave certain old age pensioners the guaranteed income supplement, certain consequences flowed and from that time on all hon. members have felt these consequences. First of all, there was a feeling of ill will on the part of those now being paid the $80 because the 2 per cent cost of living increase was not provided at that time. There has been a feeling of ill will on the part of those in receipt of the guaranteed income supplement because some people, by not declaring income, may be able to obtain more than their rightful share of the supplement. As a result, we do not have the type of atmosphere we want to create for our old age pensioners. Instead, we have had divisiveness, ill feeling among the different classes of old age pensioners and resentment, on the part of many who do not receive it, of those who do.
I suggest the same consequences will flow from the family allowance legislation now before the House. We will have a division of our working people. There will be a polarization in that some people will get none of the benefits of family allowances yet will pay a large proportion of the cost. If there is one thing we do not need, Mr. Speaker, it is division among the working people who are dependent on their income. I am rather surprised that the minister would seek to introduce this legislation at this time. I shall continue in depth tomorrow afternoon, if I may call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-SUGGESTED ONGOING PROGRAM TO ASSIST PEOPLE IN ISOLATED COMMUNITIES
MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-SUGGESTED ONGOING PROGRAM TO ASSIST PEOPLE IN ISOLATED COMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time ago I asked a question in the House of the acting minister of manpower and immigration regarding consideration being given to extending the Local Initiatives Program. I asked the question in sincerity because in my opinion this is the first time citizens of Canada in remote and isolated communities have been able to use their initiative on behalf of their communities to create employment opportunities for those in need.
However, through lack of communication in the past many people in remote areas were unable to involve themselves in the programs of the government. This is the reason I should like to have this program extended. Unfortunately, the minister merely replied that the province of Newfoundland received its fair share. I am not satisfied with this answer because regardless of the fair share of anyone in Canada, there are unemployed people in remote and isolated communities of Newfoundland who have never had the opportunity to participate in government programs because of lack of communication. The people in the isolated communities of my province do not receive the message of government programs. I feel communication is vital in this regard in spite of the weaknesses in some of the programs.
In spite of the fact that the Local Initiatives Program has done some good, I believe the government has failed to help those who are unemployed and are in greatest need. There has seemed to be lack of control by the government over the program in respect of going to the Manpower centres and finding out who indeed is in need of a job. I give the government credit for introducing the program, but if the government is prepared to provide such a program I feel it should follow through to ensure that it benefits those who are in greatest need.
I spoke to the parliamentary secretary and it was indicated to me that some of these programs may be ongoing. I believe the program is good and I feel there is no reason it should not be continued so that people whose programs have been disapproved could have the opportunity to receive the benefit of an ongoing program which would create employment opportunities for those who are vitally in need in my province. I can only say I hope consideration will be given to some other type of program such as the Local Initiatives Program.
People in one community ask me why a project has been approved in another community as being a good one while in their community a similar project has been disapproved. I can only say to them that this is because many programs were submitted and there was lack of control. I believe the parliamentary secretary or the minister would wish to clarify this situation so that I may give proper answers to these people. I say, again, this is a good program but for some reason people across Canada wonder why they cannot participate while others have an opportunity to participate in a similar program. I ask the parliamentary secretary to clarify this matter and give me an indication of what the future holds for these Canadians.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-SUGGESTED ONGOING PROGRAM TO ASSIST PEOPLE IN ISOLATED COMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party for the strong support he has given to the Local Initiatives Program. This program is just that; it is a program based on local initiatives. Despite reports to the contrary, the Salvation Army was given a grant in Burlington, Ontario, for a very worth-while social development program.
It is a fact that for every project in a metropolitan centre there are many other projects designed to provide employment and improve facilities in literally hundreds of small towns, villages and rural crossroad communities all across the country. We have projects such as the building of a community centre at 100 Mile House in the B.C. interior, land clearing and repairs to housing at Watson Lake in the Yukon, construction of a terminal building at Haven Settlement in the Northwest Territories, establishment of a fishing co-op at Savage Island in northern Manitoba, construction of a community wharf at White Bay, Newfoundland, community rink improvements at Forchu, Nova Scotia.
The list goes on and on. Indeed, while I have many more examples such as those I have given, I cannot give the whole list of perhaps not very glamorous but nevertheless very important contributions to community betterment and alleviation of unemployment represented by the hundreds of projects put forward by community groups in isolated settlements which have been accepted under this program. I cannot give the list simply because what may be regarded as an isolated community by people in one place may be seen as the very heart of civilization to those living somewhere else. But one thing I can tell the House is that LIP has been very successful in directing aid to pockets of unemployment wherever they exist in the country.
It is common knowledge, of course, that in absolute numbers most of our unemployed live in cities of 50,000, 100,000 or more population. But while the numbers are not so great, it is unfortunately often true that some of the more remote rural areas suffer proportionately much higher rates of unemployment in winter than do the cities. LIP has been very conscious of this problem in its allocations and, since it is a program primarily concerned with providing useful work for the unemployed, it has concentrated a good deal of effort in stimulating proposals for worth-while projects in smaller centres where unemployment is high.
In terms of the population in those geographic areas served by the various Canada Manpower centres, the centres having the highest rates of unemployment, which had an estimated 30 per cent of the country's total unemployed, received nearly 40 per cent of project approvals and funds. Those with the lowest unemployment rates, which generally tended to be the more populous places, the Canada Manpower centre areas having the lowest rates of unemployment in the country, accounted for 25 per cent of total unemployment and received 15 per cent of project approvals and funds. Of course, in all areas some rationing of funds was necessary and not every project could be approved. But given the emphasis I have described, an emphasis which was maintained for reasons

which I hope I have made clear, applications from rural areas were given consideration commensurate with local unemployment conditions.
New employment creating programs are under consideration and the experience gained in the Local Initiatives Program, both as to the source of the applications received and the type of projects put forward, will be taken into account in this consideration.

TRADE-DISPLAY OF CANADIAN AGRICULTURAL PROJECTS AT PEKING FAIR
speechtext:
I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that you shall not hear such rapid-fire speaking as that to which you have just listened. I suppose it works on the old theory that if you talk fast enough somebody will believe you.
I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) last fall a question pertaining to the China Solo Fair and at that time I did not receive the answer that I was seeking. The minister announced in a news release that Canada was going to have an important China Solo Fair which would be the first fair at which Canadian goods would be the only goods on display.
I then asked the minister if there would be any attempt to show Canadian agricultural products at this fair. At that time there was no answer. Therefore, in the new session I once again asked the question and the minister suggested that there were 250 companies or groups desirous of participating in the China Solo Fair. He did not outline what those companies were and whether any of them were connected with the agricultural industry. The information I am seeking through my questions is simple: Who has applied? Will there be a display of our agricultural products?
In his answer the other day the minister suggested that the Canadian Wheat Board has a direct line of communication with a purchasing agency in China. I think a number of points should be made about that type of answer. For example, one large sale of wheat should not ignore the possibility of further development of sales on a long-term basis. This is particularly true now that the Americans are developing friendship with the Chinese and say that they will trade in non-strategic goods and products. That, to me, means agricultural products, making the Chinese Solo Fair that much more important in terms of displaying our agricultural products.
I am concerned that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce assumes that there is only one farm product to be sold to the Chinese. I point out to him that there are a variety of products such as beef, rapeseed oil, mutton, dairy products, sunflower seed oil, other grains, etc., that we should display and which would be of interest to the Chinese buying companies.
In terms of the answers I have received, I wonder whether the government has ever considered the difficulty involved in having one minister in charge of the Wheat

Board and another in charge of trade and commerce, when at times those two gentlemen have jurisdiction in the same area of trade affecting the sale of Canadian agricultural products. I ask the government that the Canadian people be informed of who has applied and who will be going to the Chinese Solo Fair. I hope the agricultural sector will not be ignored because of the minister's preoccupation with the industrial sector.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bruce Howard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRADE-DISPLAY OF CANADIAN AGRICULTURAL PROJECTS AT PEKING FAIR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me assure the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) that Canada will be represented in all important aspects of its commercial and agricultural sectors at the Solo Canadian Trade Fair in Peking.

maintopic: TRADE-DISPLAY OF CANADIAN AGRICULTURAL PROJECTS AT PEKING FAIR
speechtext: What about agricultural products?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRADE-DISPLAY OF CANADIAN AGRICULTURAL PROJECTS AT PEKING FAIR
speechtext:
I included agricultural products. Canada is in the position of going to China as a guest of the Chinese government, and all exhibits at the fair will be entered in consultation with the Chinese government. Exhibits will include grains, oils seeds, forage seeds, tobacco, livestock and semen, and poultry breeding stock. We will have a very large exhibit in this area that will be backed up by technical experts with films and teams of experts who will be available to talk to the Chinese specialists in these fields.
We expect that our specialists will also be touring areas of China which are involved in agricultural production and areas that are of special interest to Canadian producers. We hope that as a result of this presentation we will be able to enlarge our sphere of influence in the agricultural field in China. But I emphasize that these arrangements with the Chinese government must be carried out in consultation with the Chinese with respect to the selection of products that will be shown.
I repeat that we will be represented in the agricultural field. The displays will be made by representatives of national producer and trade associations and marketing boards, and not by private companies as in the case of manufactured products. In this way we feel we will have the most effective representatives there, that we will be able to obtain immediate business in this area and will be able to open up areas of trade that will be of long-term significance for Canada and Canada's farmers.

maintopic: YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH-REQUEST FOR OTHER PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT
YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH-REQUEST FOR OTHER PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is typical of our situation that in again raising the question of employment for youth this summer the minister has not thought it important to be here to deal with the questions that I have been putting to him week after week. It is typical, in view of his non-answer to my question this afternoon and to questions over the last weeks and months that have attempted to find out what the government's answer is to the growing problem and national crisis of summer employment for the nation's youth.
On March 9, commenting on the Cohen report which followed last summer's Opportunities for Youth and other
March 27, 1972

programs and which pointed out a major failure to solve student unemployment programs, I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) if he was now exploring with the provinces or with business and other authorities further measures that might be taken to alleviate the very serious student unemployment that will occur this coming summer. The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, we are exploring all possible means to reduce unemployment.
I would not even dignify that response by calling it an intelligent or concerned answer. On March 22, again inquiring what would happen to the many project submissions that could not be accepted by Opportunities for Youth-some 16,000-I asked:
In view of the fact the minister indicated earlier that some 20,000 opportunities for youth projects have now been submitted and only a fraction of these will be accepted, is there any specific program underway to consult with other agencies that might well implement some of these very worthwhile projects?
The minister replied: "Yes, Mr. Speaker". Again today, in a series of specific questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) I asked a question about this coming summer and expected massive youth unemployment but did not receive an answer.
The government, and particularly the Secretary of State, seem to be content to play parliamentary games at a time when more and more young people are seeking employment on a labour market that has neither the depth nor the scope to accommodate a substantial portion of them. It now appears clear that there may be over a quarter of a million young people with no chance of employment. The reticence and lack of concern by the ministry and this government is shocking. This is difficult to understand because as far back as last fall, one series of unemployment figures which was published showed a higher proportion of unemployed young people between the ages of 14 and 24. The Prime Minister seemed surprised and disturbed by this.
The Prime Minister obviously had not been reading Economic Council of Canada reports over the years which have been consistently warning the government to expect this influx of young people into the labour force as the baby boom of the 1940s reached the working age level. In September, 1969, the Economic Council of Canada reported:
There is a need to develop much more effective measures to bridge the present disturbing gap between school enrolment and productive employment, especially with very large numbers of young people emerging from the educational system.
That can be said both of those coming permanently on the labour market and those who are seeking seasonal employment in order to further their education. The government is still not aware of the figures relating to lack of employment. There will be over 1,300,000 young people available this summer, an increase of 100,000 over last year. How well did the government do last year? According to this evaluation report tabled last Friday, about 75 per cent of the young people seeking work last summer found it in the private sector. Of the remaining 25 per cent, about 5 per cent found employment through federal government expenditure, which leaves about 20 per cent who found no employment. That is about 217,000 young people unemployed last summer. If we add the projected
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
increase of 100,000, it is not difficult to assume that there will be over a quarter of a million young people unemployed this summer.
In trying to brush this off last November 11 the Prime Minister suggested that many young people would just as soon bum around. I have news for the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State: those who hitch-hiked around then or now are not counted as seeking work or as statistics for unemployment. Who knows how many simply turned to bumming around because there was no promise of employment? The Prime Minister's ability to slough off serious issues of work opportunity constitutes, in the vernacular, a bum steer, a steer from which our young people deserve escape.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH-REQUEST FOR OTHER PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Shame!

maintopic: YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH-REQUEST FOR OTHER PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The minister seemed reluctant to be quite so eulogistic about opportunities for this year, and rightly so. He must now realize that Opportunities for Youth is no solution to the problem of growing youth unemployment in this country. Close to 200,000 young people will willingly spend time and energy in thinking out proposals. They will submit them in the expectation of seeing those projects accepted. How many of those young people, and there are almost 200,000 of them, will be fortunate? How many projects will receive favourable consideration within a few weeks? I suggest that less than 30,000 will be in that position. Therefore, over 160,000 young people at that late date will be forced to find other means of employment.
That is a cruel if not a close to dishonest way, of dealing with young people who are anxious to further their own position and prepare themselves for the service of this country in a social and economic way. This entails a waste of youthful talent and a serious waste of youthful expectations and is bound to create growing frustration and cynicism.
We face a major dilemma in this country, one which this government has not yet recognized. We need an over-all strategy for coping with the situation. Hopefully, through that strategy some leadership can be shown by this government. Today there is no evidence of such leadership, which is necessary for co-ordinating the activities of various levels of government and of various bodies, public and private. Only with such bodies acting together can we put together an over-all plan. Only that way, if we act on a long-term basis, can we help our young people to work constructively for this country and at the same time for their own advancement, and help them avoid that despair which the leadership of the government and of the minister has not alleviated.

In response to the question of initiatives being taken by the government to tackle the problem of student unemployment, the hon. member previously had an extensive exchange with the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) on this question in the miscellaneous estimates committee on March 17. I do not see the need to comment further on steps we have taken to secure the co-operation of the provinces in an all-government effort to deal with student summer unemployment.
With regard to the private sector, it has become apparent that individual companies and agencies are interested in funding projects which, although extremely worth while, are not eligible for funding by Opportunities for Youth. Thus, a special committee is working this year to follow up these initial contacts made with the private sector and also to seek out and encourage other companies or agencies who might be interested in such a venture. Where possible, projects are referred to these sponsors.
However, the summer programs which cure funded by the Department of the Secretary of State should not in any way be misconstrued as representing total government action towards alleviating student summer unemployment. Appreciating that the traditional source of student employment lies with the private sector, the
Department of Manpower will continue to work with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in its Operation Placement program. The department's role will be to encourage co-operation among all the Chamber's 125,000 members across the country to develop local campaigns and promote community involvement in providing summer employment.
In addition, $1,773,000 has been allocated to fund 132 special Canada Manpower centres for students. These centres will be staffed by 500 students and will be able to assist both students seeking employment in industry, and industry seeking students to fill job openings. I might also point to a new program this summer in the Department of Manpower-the inter-regional student summer employment program. Through this program students seeking employment in other provinces will be assisted by government.
The government is aware that this program will not by itself solve the problem of student unemployment. However, both in the example it sets and by the model it portrays it represents a major effort by the government to involve the provinces, the private sector and other authorities in a co-ordinated and comprehensive response to student unemployment problems.
